Americans also say 'dress-down Friday' or 'we can dress down' for relaxed clothing at work. A natural reply to being dressed down is 'I understand, it won't happen again.'

distinctions.note: A reprimand is formal and often official or written, while to dress someone down is informal and spoken.
Scold suggests correcting a child or pet, while dress down suggests a sharp rebuke from an adult or boss.

collocations: dress down in front of colleagues

examples.everyday: My dad really dressed me down when I came home after midnight.
examples.professional: The director dressed him down in the meeting for missing the release deadline.
examples.analytical: Dressing someone down in public may correct behavior, but it often damages the trust needed for learning.

nuance.analogy: Being dressed down is like standing in a rainstorm of words that leaves you soaked.
nuance.etymology: Dress in the sense 'to arrange or scold' combined with the adverb down.
common_mistakes: Using 'dress down' as a noun; say 'a dressing down' or 'a dress-down' instead.
Mixing up the two senses: in a sentence about clothes, the phrase does not mean scolding.

senses.definition: Having splayfoot; habitually standing or walking with the ends of the feet angled outward.
senses.example: The toddler was duck-footed, so the pediatrician recommended special shoes.

core.definition: Having feet that turn outward, so that a person stands or walks with the toes pointing out to the sides.

pronunciation.tip: Stress FOOT, the main word, and make the ending -ed a short id sound. Keep the first syllable quick and light, as in 'duck.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive. It can sound mildly unkind if used as a teasing remark about someone's walk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'duck-footed' in everyday speech. In casual talk they say 'toes turned out' or 'walks with his toes out.' 'Pigeon-toed' is the common American term for the opposite: feet turned inward. 'Duck-footed' appears more often in medical, dance, or descriptive writing.

distinctions.note: 'Pigeon-toed' means the toes point inward; 'duck-footed' means the toes point outward.
'Bowlegged' describes legs curved outward at the knees; 'duck-footed' describes the direction of the feet.

examples.everyday: My brother has always been a bit duck-footed, so his walk looks like a little waddle.
examples.professional: The physical therapist noted that the patient was duck-footed, which changed our gait assessment.
examples.analytical: The sculptor kept the duck-footed stance of the figure, a detail that gives the statue an odd dignity.

nuance.analogy: Like a duck waddling, with its feet pointing out to either side.
nuance.etymology: From duck (the bird) plus footed, referring to the outward-turned feet of ducks.
common_mistakes: Using 'duck-footed' for inward-turned feet; the American term for that is 'pigeon-toed'.
Leaving out the hyphen in writing; the usual form is 'duck-footed.'

senses.definition: Any member of a race of beings from (especially Scandinavian and other Germanic) folklore, usually depicted as having some sort of supernatural powers and being skilled in crafting and metalworking, often as short with long beards, and sometimes as clashing with elves.
senses.example: In the old stories, a dwarf forged a magic sword deep inside the mountain.

senses.definition: A person of short stature, often one whose limbs are disproportionately small in relation to the body as compared with typical adults, usually as the result of a genetic condition.
senses.example: Her cousin, who is a dwarf, has a successful career as an architect in Chicago.

senses.definition: An animal, plant or other thing much smaller than the usual of its sort.
senses.example: dwarf tree

senses.definition: A dwarf star.
senses.example: Astronomers measured the mass of the white dwarf to estimate its cooling rate.

senses.definition: To render (much) smaller, turn into a dwarf (version).
senses.example: The new skyscraper will dwarf the historic church beside it.

senses.definition: To make appear (much) smaller, puny, tiny; to be much larger than.
senses.example: The newly-built skyscraper dwarfs all older buildings in the downtown skyline.

senses.definition: To make appear insignificant.
senses.example: Bach dwarfs all other composers.

senses.definition: To become (much) smaller.
senses.example: During the drought, the reservoir began to dwarf, shrinking dramatically each month.

senses.definition: To hinder from growing to the natural size; to make or keep small; to stunt.
senses.example: Severe malnutrition in childhood can dwarf a child's growth permanently.

senses.definition: Miniature.
senses.example: The specimen is a very dwarf form of the plant.

core.definition: To make something look small or insignificant by comparison, or to tower over and overshadow it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the only syllable. The w is clearly pronounced at the start, and the vowel is the American 'aw' sound, which is the same in cot and caught. Keep the r strong at the end, and do not add a vowel after the f.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in the verb sense, but the noun for a person is considered offensive and is outdated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'the new tower dwarfs everything else on the skyline' or 'his talent dwarfs mine' in ordinary and professional talk. For people, do not use 'dwarf' as a noun in everyday conversation; say 'a person with dwarfism' or 'a little person', which is the respectful American usage. In science, 'dwarf planet' and 'dwarf star' are normal technical terms.

distinctions.note: Overshadow means to make something seem less important, often by being more prominent, while dwarf implies a clear difference in size or scale.
Tower over is literal and physical, while dwarf can also describe abstract comparisons like money, skill or achievement.
Outshine stresses being brighter or better, while dwarf stresses being much bigger or more impressive in scale.

examples.everyday: The new stadium completely dwarfs the old one, and you can see it from the highway.
examples.professional: Our Q4 revenue dwarfs last year's numbers, so the board wants to fund more hiring.
examples.analytical: Modern cosmic scales dwarf human experience, a fact that unsettles theologies centered on a human-scaled universe.

nuance.analogy: Like a giant oak standing beside a row of saplings.
nuance.etymology: From Old English dweorg, a word of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Using 'dwarf' as a noun for people in everyday American conversation, which is considered offensive.
Pronouncing it as 'dwahf' with a flat a; the American vowel is the 'aw' sound.
Dropping the w sound at the start of the word.

dwarf.etymology: From Middle English *dwergh*, *dwerw*, *dwerf*, from Old English *dweorg*, from **dwerg*, from Proto-Germanic **dwergaz*.

senses.definition: Approaching death; about to die; moribund.
senses.example: The dying dog was put out of his misery with a single shot!

senses.definition: Declining, terminal, or drawing to an end.
senses.example: In the dying moments of daylight I glimpsed a sail on the horizon.

senses.definition: Pertaining to death, or the moments before death.
senses.example: His dying words were of his mother.

senses.definition: The process of approaching death; loss of life; death.
senses.example: Her grandmother spoke openly about dying and wanted to be at home.

core.definition: Near death or about to die; also used to describe something that is coming to an end.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a light 'ing' with a reduced vowel. Non-native speakers often lengthen the -ing sound or stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative in its literal sense of approaching death, but very casual when used for exaggeration, as in 'I'm dying for coffee'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'dying' literally for people at the end of life, as in 'a dying patient', and casually as hyperbole. The phrase 'I'm dying' means 'I find it extremely funny' or 'I want this very much', which is informal and common. Avoid joking about death in formal or sensitive situations, such as with a grieving family.

distinctions.note: Dead means no longer alive, while dying means in the process of dying and not yet dead.
Terminal is a formal medical term for a disease expected to cause death, whereas dying is the everyday word for someone close to death.

examples.everyday: I'm dying for a cup of coffee right now, so let's stop at the next place.
examples.professional: The old reporting tool is dying, so we are moving everything to the new dashboard next quarter.
examples.analytical: Theologians have long asked what the dying person experiences in the final moments before death, and how the soul relates to the body in that transition.

nuance.analogy: A dying flame is like a candle burning low, still lit but clearly moving toward going out.
nuance.etymology: From die, from Old Norse deyja, meaning 'to die', with the present participle -ing.
common_mistakes: Using 'dying' in a serious context as a joke, which can sound insensitive to Americans.
Saying 'I am dying of hunger' casually; Americans more often say 'I'm starving' or 'I'm dying for something to eat'.

senses.definition: A Christian feast commemorating the resurrection of Jesus Christ. It is celebrated on the first Sunday (and Monday) following the full moon that occurs on or next after the vernal equinox, ranging in most of Western Christianity (such as Protestantism and Roman Catholicism) from March 22 to April 25, and in Eastern Christianity (such as the Coptic Church and Eastern Orthodox Church) from April 4 to May 8.
senses.example: We spent each of the past five Easters together as a family.

senses.definition: Eastertide (“the period from Easter to Whitsun”).
senses.example: Our church hosts a special choir concert every Sunday throughout Easter, from the feast until Pentecost.

senses.definition: Usually preceded by an inflection of make: the act of receiving the Eucharist during Easter.
senses.example: My grandmother insisted that everyone make their Easter before the week ended, going to confession first.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of Easter term.
A festival held in honor of the goddess Eostre or Ostara, celebrated at the vernal equinox or within the month of April; Eostre, Ostara.
senses.example: Ancient Germanic peoples celebrated Easter at the spring equinox to honor the goddess Eostre.

senses.definition: To celebrate Easter.
senses.example: Our family plans to Easter quietly at home this year, with a simple dinner and no travel.

senses.definition: To spend the Easter season in some place.
senses.example: My parents Eastered in Florence, touring churches and museums through the spring holiday.

core.definition: The Christian feast celebrating Jesus Christ's resurrection, observed on a Sunday in spring, usually in March or April.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -er is a reduced, r-colored vowel, so do not say EES-tur or EES-tah.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It is a major holiday and a greeting; in shops and offices, Happy Easter is said widely.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say Happy Easter to friends, neighbors and coworkers, even when they are not religious. Easter Sunday is the day itself, and many people also use Easter weekend for the holiday break. Secular symbols like Easter eggs and the Easter Bunny are common. Protestants often say Resurrection Sunday in church contexts.

distinctions.note: Passover is the Jewish feast commemorating the Exodus from Egypt; it often falls close to Easter but is a separate festival.
Pascha is the name Eastern Christians use for the feast, from Hebrew pesach, Passover.
Resurrection Sunday is a common term in some Protestant churches; Easter is the everyday American name.

examples.everyday: We are having ham and potatoes for Easter dinner at my sister's house this year.
examples.professional: Our company is closed on Easter Monday, so please plan the release for the week before.
examples.analytical: The date of Easter, set by the paschal full moon, ties the Christian feast to the lunar and solar calendars.

nuance.analogy: Like a hinge on the Christian year, where Holy Week and the spring season turn.
nuance.etymology: From Old English ēastre, a name of uncertain origin; the Greek and Latin name is pascha, from Hebrew pesach.
common_mistakes: Saying EES-tur or ASS-ter, which drops the r or changes the vowel.
Writing easter in lowercase; the holiday name is always capitalized.
nuance.biblical_note: The English word Easter does not occur in the Revised Standard Version. The Greek word pascha, from the Hebrew pesach (Passover), stands behind the feast. Acts 12:4 uses Passover for the Jewish feast, which Christians later linked with the resurrection. Matthew 28:6 reports the angel telling the women that Jesus is not in the tomb because he has risen. 1 Corinthians 5:7 calls Christ our paschal lamb who has been sacrificed.

traditions.view: Eastern Orthodox Christians call the feast Pascha and compute its date with the Julian calendar, so it often falls later than in the West. The Easter vigil on the night before is the central liturgy and includes the proclamation of the resurrection.

Roman Catholics use the Gregorian calendar and the same rule as Western churches: Easter is the first Sunday after the paschal full moon on or after the spring equinox. The Easter Vigil is the principal liturgy of the feast.

Most Protestant churches follow the Western date and celebrate Easter as the central feast of the church year. Lutherans, Anglicans and Reformed churches keep the feast in formal worship, while Baptists and Pentecostals often focus on the empty tomb in preaching; some Protestant groups observe it with little liturgy.

easter.etymology: The noun is derived from Middle English *ester*, from Old English *ēastre*, seemingly from *Ēastre*, a proposed Anglo-Saxon goddess of the dawn whose festival is thought to have been celebrated around the vernal equinox.

senses.definition: Any persistent wind from the east (usually a broad current or belt of easterly winds).
senses.example: A steady easterly blew off the harbor all week, bringing cold fog to the coast.

senses.definition: Coming from the east; originating in the east.
senses.example: an easterly wind

senses.definition: Facing the east; directed towards the east.
senses.example: an easterly course

senses.definition: Located towards or in the east.
senses.example: the easterly side of the lake

senses.definition: In an eastward direction or position; towards the east.
senses.example: The storm drifted easterly across the bay before turning north toward the coast.

senses.definition: From the east.
senses.example: The cold air came easterly off the Atlantic and settled over the town all night.

core.definition: Coming from the east, or moving toward the east; used especially of winds that blow from the east.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, EE-ster-lee. The t between vowels is flapped so it sounds like a soft d, and the final -ly is a light ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive; it is a precise directional word used mainly in weather and navigation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use easterly mostly for winds, as in 'an easterly wind' or 'easterly winds expected tomorrow' in a forecast. For a general direction, people usually say 'east' or 'to the east.' When describing location rather than wind, 'eastern' is the usual word.

distinctions.note: Easterly describes the direction a wind comes from or moves; eastern describes the location or character of a place.
Eastward describes motion toward the east and is used more for travel and direction than for wind.

examples.everyday: Feel that? The wind has turned easterly, so it's going to get cold tonight.
examples.professional: The forecast calls for an easterly flow along the coast, so the sea breeze will be weaker this afternoon.
examples.analytical: The easterly trade winds shaped early Atlantic navigation routes, which is why ships sailed west on one path and returned on another.

nuance.analogy: Like a weather vane that points to where the wind is coming from: easterly tells you the source, not the destination.
nuance.etymology: From Old English ēast (east) with the suffix -erly, meaning in the direction of.
common_mistakes: Saying 'the wind is east' instead of 'the wind is easterly' or 'the wind is from the east'
Adding an extra syllable, pronouncing it as EE-ster-uh-lee

senses.definition: The quality of being easygoing.

core.definition: The quality of being relaxed, tolerant and unfussy; a calm temperament that does not get easily upset.

pronunciation.tip: Stress GOH as the main syllable, with a lighter stress on the first ee. The -ing is short, and the ending -ness is reduced to nus.

nuance.connotation: Positive, describing a relaxed and agreeable temperament, though it can imply a lack of concern in some contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans far more often use the adjective easygoing, as in 'She's really easygoing,' rather than the noun. Easygoingness is rare and sounds stiff in conversation. In everyday speech, say 'She has an easygoing personality' instead.

distinctions.note: Easygoing is the normal adjective and is far more common in American speech.
Laid-back is informal and suggests a casual style; easygoingness is a more general and slightly formal quality.
Tolerance means accepting differences, while easygoingness describes a relaxed temperament that rarely gets upset.

examples.professional: His easygoingness made him a good mediator in project meetings, though it sometimes let decisions drift.
examples.analytical: Some philosophers treat easygoingness as a virtue, but it can slide into indifference when the stakes are high.

nuance.analogy: Like a loose sail that catches any breeze without strain: relaxed rather than rigid.
nuance.etymology: Formed from easygoing (easy plus going) with the noun suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Using easygoingness in everyday speech where easygoing is more natural
Writing easy going as two words when the adjective is written as one word, easygoing

senses.definition: In an efficient or effective manner; with powerful effect.
senses.example: The new filter effectively removed the sediment from the river water.

senses.definition: Essentially, in effect, for all practical purposes.
senses.example: On paper, the answer seems to be yes, but, effectively, the answer is no.

core.definition: In a way that successfully produces the result wanted; or, for all practical purposes, essentially.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, FEK. The middle syllable is reduced to a quick 'iv', and the ending is a light 'lee', not a long 'ly'.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing success, and neutral when it means 'essentially'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use effectively in workplace language and everyday conversation: 'We handled that effectively' or 'Effectively, we're finished.' The second sense, 'essentially', is common in speech and writing, often with a pause before it. Effectively is a standard, polished choice, while effectually sounds archaic to most Americans.

distinctions.note: Effectually is formal and rare in American speech, and is used for achieving the desired result; effectively is the everyday choice.
Essentially means fundamentally or at heart, while effectively in the second sense means for all practical purposes, even if not technically true.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor handled the snowstorm effectively, clearing the whole driveway before anyone else was awake.
examples.professional: Since the project lead left, Priya has effectively been running the team, though her title hasn't changed yet.
examples.analytical: Since the contract binds both parties from signing, the amendment is effectively a new agreement, whatever the document calls it.

nuance.analogy: If a coach is effectively in charge, the title may say assistant, but the team follows her every call.
nuance.etymology: From effective plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using effectively to mean 'efficiently' in the sense of speed or economy.
Putting the stress on the last syllable, which makes the word sound foreign.

senses.definition: A liquid outpouring.
An outpouring of speech or emotion.
Process of gases passing through a hole or holes considerably smaller than the mean free path of the gas molecules.
senses.example: Effusion through a tiny orifice follows Graham's law, so lighter gases escape faster.

senses.definition: The seeping of fluid into a body cavity; the fluid itself.
senses.example: pleural effusion

core.definition: A sudden, unrestrained outpouring of emotion or words, or a liquid flowing out of something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, FYOO. The 'sion' ending is pronounced like 'zhun', not 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing warmth or affection; can feel excessive when it describes emotion or speech that is overflowing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use effusion mostly in writing, formal speech, or literary description, such as a writer describing a gushing display of gratitude. In casual talk, people say something like 'she just gushed' or 'he went on and on'. The medical and scientific sense, a fluid leaking into a body cavity, is used in clinical settings.

distinctions.note: An outburst is usually a sudden, brief explosion of anger or laughter, while an effusion is a longer, more flowing outpouring of feeling or words.
Emission is the neutral release of something, such as gas or light, while effusion often implies abundance and warmth in emotional or verbal contexts.

examples.everyday: When I told my grandmother about the new baby, she gave me an effusion of hugs and tears.
examples.professional: The client's email was an effusion of praise for the team, though it did not address the budget problem.
examples.analytical: Wordsworth's poetry often turns a quiet observation into an effusion of feeling that spills beyond the scene itself.

nuance.analogy: Like a bottle of soda shaken and opened, an effusion bursts out in a flood rather than trickling.
nuance.etymology: From Latin effusio, from effundere, to pour out.
common_mistakes: Using effusion as a verb; the verb is effuse, and the adjective is effusive.
Pronouncing the ending as 'shun' instead of 'zhun'.

senses.definition: Form; essence; type; species.

core.definition: In Plato's philosophy, the eternal form or essence that makes a thing what it is and that many particular things share.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. Many Americans pronounce the final sound as a short 'ahs', not 'ohs', because of the cot-caught merger.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a technical term in philosophy with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use eidos almost only in philosophy classes, scholarship, and discussion of Plato, Aristotle, or Husserl. In ordinary conversation they would say 'essence' or 'form.' Use it only when you are discussing those thinkers or need the precise technical sense.

distinctions.note: Essence is a general English word for the core nature of something; eidos is the specific Platonic term for an eternal form.
Form is common and can mean shape; eidos is a philosophical term for an intelligible essence beyond appearance.

examples.everyday: My friend who studies philosophy keeps talking about the eidos of a chair, which sounds strange at dinner.
examples.professional: In the design review, we need to identify the eidos of the product, the one feature every version must keep.
examples.analytical: Aristotle criticized Plato's view that the eidos exists apart from the particulars that instantiate it.

nuance.analogy: An eidos is like the blueprint of a house: every house built from it shares its design, though none is the blueprint itself.
nuance.etymology: From Greek eidos, 'form, shape, kind', related to the verb 'to see'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'EE-dos' as in Spanish; Americans say 'EYE-dahs'.
Using it as a synonym for any kind of form or shape in everyday English.

core.definition: A Hebrew name for God, usually translated 'God Almighty', which stresses God's power and sufficiency. It appears in Genesis and Exodus.

pronunciation.tip: Say 'el' with a short e, then stress the second word on its last syllable: 'shah-DYE'. Americans often stress the first word, which is wrong here. The 'sh' is a clear American sh sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive and reverent. It is used in worship, Bible study, and theology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this name mainly in churches, Bible studies, and sermons, and in music such as the song 'El Shaddai' from Filipino Catholic charismatic worship. In casual speech people more often say 'God' or 'the Almighty'. Saying the name in a public setting is natural in religious contexts and sounds stiff or odd outside them.

distinctions.note: Elohim is the common Hebrew word for God, used broadly. El Shaddai emphasizes God's might and is linked to the patriarchs.
Yahweh is the personal covenant name of God, usually rendered LORD in English Bibles. El Shaddai is a title that stresses power, not the covenant name.

examples.everyday: At church last Sunday, the pastor said God revealed himself to Abraham as El Shaddai, which means God Almighty.
examples.professional: In my course on the Pentateuch, I teach that El Shaddai in Genesis 17 marks a new covenantal revelation to Abram.
examples.analytical: Exodus 6:3 distinguishes the patriarchs' knowledge of God as El Shaddai from the fuller revelation of the name LORD, a distinction that shapes the theology of the divine name.

nuance.analogy: Like a title such as 'the Almighty' that names a person by their power, El Shaddai names God by his strength.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew el ('God') and Shaddai, whose meaning is uncertain; traditional renderings include 'Almighty' and 'the Mountain One'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first word, 'EL shaddai', instead of the second.
Treating Shaddai as a common English word; it is a proper name element in Hebrew.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew is El Shaddai, from el ('God') and Shaddai. In Genesis 17:1, God appears to Abram and says he is God Almighty, El Shaddai, and calls Abram to walk before him blamelessly. In Genesis 35:11, God uses the same name in blessing Jacob. In Exodus 6:3, God says he appeared to the patriarchs as God Almighty but was not known to them by the name LORD.

senses.definition: The collective people of a country, state, or electoral district who are entitled to vote.
senses.example: The votes have been counted and the electorate has spoken.

senses.definition: (historical) The office, or area of dominion, of an Elector (“a German prince entitled to elect the emperor of the Holy Roman Empire”); an electorship.
senses.example: In 1356 the Golden Bull confirmed the electorate of Bohemia among the seven princes' rights.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: The people in a country, state, or district who are entitled to vote in an election.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, LEK. The final -ate is a reduced, unstressed syllable, and the r is pronounced clearly in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a group of voters, usually in political or news contexts, and carries no positive or negative judgment by itself.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use electorate mainly in political news, civics, and analysis, as in 'the electorate is divided.' In casual talk people usually say 'voters' or 'the public.' The word is almost always used as a singular collective noun, even for a large group.

distinctions.note: Voters are individual people who vote; electorate is the whole group considered as one body.
A constituency is a specific district with its own representative; electorate is broader and can refer to a whole country or state.

examples.everyday: I don't think the electorate really understands how the Electoral College works.
examples.professional: Our polling data shows the electorate in the suburbs is shifting toward early voting.
examples.analytical: A democratic system depends on whether the electorate can form judgments on evidence rather than on partisan loyalty alone.

nuance.analogy: Think of the electorate as a single jury: it is made up of many people, but it is treated as one body that delivers a verdict at the ballot box.
nuance.etymology: From Latin elector, 'one who chooses', from eligere, 'to choose'.
common_mistakes: Using electorate for one voter; it refers to the whole group.
Saying 'the electorates are' in ordinary American usage, when 'the electorate is' is standard.
patterns: the electorate (+ singular or plural verb)

senses.definition: The process of obscuring information to make it unreadable without special knowledge, key files, or passwords.
senses.example: Encryption protects our customer data while it moves across the public internet.

senses.definition: A ciphertext, a cryptogram, an encrypted value. Usually used with the preposition "of" followed by the value that is hidden in it.
senses.example: The cryptographer compared the encryption of her message against the original.

core.definition: The process of converting data into a coded form so that only people with the correct key or password can read it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, KRIP, with a short 'i' like in 'lip.' The final syllable is reduced to a weak 'un' sound, so don't say 'en-crip-tee-own.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but it often carries positive associations with security and privacy, and sometimes negative ones in debates about government access.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use encryption constantly in tech, security, and news about messaging apps, phones, and banking. In everyday speech people say 'the app uses encryption' or 'it's end-to-end encrypted.' In technical writing it is an uncountable process noun, while the result is called ciphertext.

distinctions.note: A cipher is the algorithm or method used to scramble data, while encryption is the overall process of applying it.
Encoding converts data into a different format for transmission, usually without secrecy; encryption specifically hides the content from unauthorized readers.

examples.everyday: My phone asks me to turn on encryption before it backs up my photos.
examples.professional: We need to confirm that encryption is enabled on all customer data before the audit next week.
examples.analytical: Debates about encryption often turn on a tension between individual privacy and the state's interest in lawful access.

nuance.analogy: Encryption is like locking a message in a safe: anyone can see the box, but only someone with the right key can open it.
nuance.etymology: From encrypt, from en- plus Greek kryptos, meaning hidden.
common_mistakes: Using 'encryption' to mean the coded text itself; the result is called ciphertext or an encrypted message.
Mispronouncing the middle vowel as 'crypt' with a long 'i' (-kryyypt) instead of a short 'i.'

senses.definition: In AI: A URL where an application sends requests to a model or service.
Part of a system that serves as a hook, allowing third-party code to intercept and modify behavior at that point.
senses.example: The plugin registers an endpoint that intercepts each request before it reaches the database.

senses.definition: Either of the two points at the ends of a line segment.
senses.example: The two endpoints of the segment are labeled A and B on the diagram.

senses.definition: The point in speech at which an utterance ends.
senses.example: Speech recognition struggles when the endpoint of an utterance is unclear.

senses.definition: The entity at one end of a connection.
senses.example: Each endpoint in the network must authenticate before exchanging encrypted messages.

senses.definition: Either of the two nodes of a graph of degree 1.
senses.example: In this tree, every leaf is an endpoint with exactly one incident edge.

senses.definition: A defined occurrence during the observation period of an experiment or study.
senses.example: The primary endpoint was the rate of hospitalization within thirty days of treatment.

senses.definition: The stage in a titration at which a change in the color of an indicator indicates that no more titrant should be added.
senses.example: The endpoint was reached when the solution turned faint pink after the phenolphthalein was added.

senses.definition: To detect the endpoint of an utterance.
senses.example: The recognizer endpoints each utterance after half a second of silence.

senses.definition: To determine an endpoint in a titration process.
senses.example: We endpointed the titration when the indicator turned pink, after 24.5 milliliters of base.

core.definition: In AI and software: a URL or address where an application sends requests to access a model or service.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on END, the first word, as in most compound nouns. Pronounce both the d and the p clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical, with no emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Developers and engineers use endpoint constantly for APIs, cloud services and model serving. In a team chat you might say 'the endpoint is returning a 500 error'. Outside technology, it means the final point of a line or a process. Americans rarely use 'terminal point' in technical talk.

distinctions.note: A URL is the full web address; an endpoint is the specific path that performs an operation, though the terms overlap.
The two-word form is the everyday geometry term; the one-word form is standard in software.

examples.everyday: The app stopped working after the server moved, so the endpoint it calls has a new address.
examples.professional: Can you confirm the inference endpoint returns predictions within two hundred milliseconds before we release?
examples.analytical: The security team treats every exposed endpoint as an attack surface, so each one needs authentication and rate limits.

nuance.analogy: An endpoint is like a restaurant's pickup window: customers never see the kitchen, but they can place and receive orders there.
nuance.etymology: From English end and point, the compound later adopted in software.
common_mistakes: Writing it as two words, 'end point', in technical documents.
Putting the main stress on POINT, as in 'end-POINT'.

conversation.text: Each model version gets its own endpoint, so clients can pin a specific version.
The inference endpoint scales to zero when there's no traffic.
The trial's primary endpoint was overall survival.
Every endpoint, including employee laptops, needs the security agent installed.

senses.definition: The state of being enshrined.
The act of enshrining or something that enshrines.
senses.example: The enshrinement of the Constitution in the state's founding document protects its citizens' rights.

core.definition: The act of honoring or protecting something by placing it in a special, respected position, such as in law or a hall of fame.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SHRINE, and the final syllable '-ment' is a weak 'mint' sound. Do not stress the -ment syllable or pronounce it as a full 'ment'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it implies honor, protection, and lasting recognition.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use enshrinement mostly in news, legal writing, and sports coverage, for example 'his enshrinement in the Hall of Fame' or 'the constitutional enshrinement of voting rights'. In everyday conversation, people usually say 'put in the Hall of Fame' or 'made official'. It sounds formal, so use it when speaking about something official or important.

distinctions.note: Recognition means acknowledging achievement or status, while enshrinement is a more formal and lasting placement within an honored system.
Installation is the formal placing of someone into an office or position, whereas enshrinement applies to honoring or protecting ideas and achievements.

examples.everyday: Her enshrinement in the local sports hall of fame made the whole town proud.
examples.professional: We're pushing for legal enshrinement of the privacy standard so it applies to every contract.
examples.analytical: The constitutional enshrinement of property rights reflects a particular theory of liberty and the state.

nuance.analogy: Like hanging a painting in a museum so that its value is recognized and protected for generations.
nuance.etymology: From enshrine, plus the noun suffix -ment, from Latin mentum via French.
common_mistakes: Stressing the final syllable (in-shrine-MENT) rather than the first syllable of the stem, SHRINE.
Using enshrinement for a simple act of keeping something; in everyday speech, 'keeping' or 'saving' is more natural.

senses.definition: Enjoying to having enjoyed entertainments; amused.

core.definition: Amused and kept interested by something enjoyable, such as a show, a game, or a conversation.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on TAYND, the second half of the word. The -ed ending is pronounced as a d sound after the n, so it is one clear beat, not two syllables.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a pleasant experience, and it is often used to say a performance or event was worth watching.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually use entertained with by, as in I was entertained by the comedian. It is a polite way to say you enjoyed something, and it works well in a review or a thank-you message after a party. Saying I was entertained is warmer than saying the show was okay.

distinctions.note: Amused suggests laughter or light humor, while entertained is broader and can mean you were kept busy or interested for a while.
Entertaining describes the thing that causes the enjoyment, while entertained describes the person who feels it.
Interested means you want to know more about something, while entertained means you enjoyed it for its own sake.

examples.everyday: Thanks for dinner, we were entertained by your stories all night.
examples.professional: Several clients said they were entertained by the demo, but they still asked for more technical detail.
examples.analytical: A reader who is entertained by a text may still resist its argument, so enjoyment and persuasion are not the same response.

nuance.analogy: Being entertained is like sitting by a campfire where the stories keep flowing, so the time passes without your noticing.
nuance.etymology: From entertain, from Old French entretenir, meaning to hold among or keep up.
common_mistakes: Using entertained for the thing rather than the person, as in The movie was entertained; the correct form is The movie was entertaining.
Forgetting the preposition by, as in I was entertained the comedian instead of I was entertained by the comedian.
patterns: entertained by sth (not before a noun)

conversation.text: The magician kept the kids entertained for an hour.
I need a good book to keep me entertained on the flight.
We were definitely entertained, but the movie made no sense.

senses.definition: One who advocates for the protection of the environment and biosphere from misuse from human activity through such measures as ecosystem protection, waste reduction and pollution prevention.
senses.example: The environmentalist testified before the county council about the proposed landfill.

senses.definition: One who holds the view that environment, rather than heredity or culture, is the primary factor in the development of an individual or group.
senses.example: As a psychologist, he was a committed environmentalist who blamed upbringing over genetics.

senses.definition: Of, or relating to environmentalism.
senses.example: The environmentalist movement grew quickly on college campuses in the 1970s.

core.definition: A person who campaigns to protect the natural environment from harm caused by human activity.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MEN, the fourth syllable. The -al- becomes a quick schwa, and the ending -ist is a short 'ist', not 'eest'.

nuance.connotation: Positive from supporters, who see the person as a protector of nature; negative from critics, who may use it to dismiss activists as political.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use environmentalist for activists, scientists and policy advocates who campaign for clean air, water and wildlife. The word can sound political, so describe someone's role more precisely if you are unsure how it will be received. The rare second sense, about environment rather than heredity shaping people, appears mainly in academic writing about development.

distinctions.note: An ecologist is a scientist who studies relationships among organisms and their habitats, while an environmentalist is an advocate who campaigns for protection.
A conservationist focuses on preserving natural resources or wildlife, while an environmentalist covers a broader range of issues, including pollution and climate.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is a real environmentalist; she composts everything and walks to work every day.
examples.professional: The environmentalist group sent a letter asking us to explain the new packaging plan before the launch.
examples.analytical: Some environmentalists argue that human activity has pushed the planet beyond natural limits, a claim that shapes policy debates.

nuance.analogy: An environmentalist is like a guard for a park, watching over the land so that it stays healthy for everyone who visits.
nuance.etymology: From environmental with the suffix -ist, 'one who advocates.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'en-vi-ron-MEN-tal-ist' with an extra syllable; say in-vy-ruhn-MEN-tuh-list.
Confusing environmentalist with ecologist in professional talk, since ecologists are scientists rather than advocates.

senses.definition: The insertion of a phoneme, letter, or syllable into a word, usually to satisfy the phonological constraints of a language or poetic context.
senses.example: The word film often gets epenthesis in speech, producing a faint vowel between the l and m.

core.definition: The addition of an extra sound, letter, or syllable inside a word, such as the b in thimble.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PEN, the second syllable, and the 'th' is voiceless, as in 'thin'. The ending '-sis' is pronounced 'sis', not 'sees'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term in linguistics and phonology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in linguistics, phonology, speech-language pathology, and language classes. It describes sounds that speakers add for ease of pronunciation, such as the p in empty, which came from an older form. Non-linguists rarely use it, and in casual talk people would simply call it an extra sound.

distinctions.note: Prothesis adds a sound at the beginning of a word, while epenthesis adds it inside the word.
Paragoge adds a sound at the end of a word, while epenthesis adds it in the middle.
Anaptyxis is a specific kind of epenthesis in which a vowel is added to break up a consonant cluster.

examples.everyday: My son says 'athalete' for athlete, which is a funny kind of epenthesis that linguists have a name for.
examples.professional: In the phonology review, we flagged an epenthesis rule that inserts a vowel into the cluster, which our speech model was mispredicting.
examples.analytical: Epenthesis shows that phonotactic constraints can override underlying forms, so a word may surface with a sound it never had in its lexical entry.

nuance.analogy: Like adding a bridge syllable so two hard-to-say sounds can meet comfortably.
nuance.etymology: From Greek epenthesis ('insertion'), from en- ('in') plus thesis ('placing').
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in EP-en-thuh-sis; the stress belongs on PEN.
Confusing epenthesis with metathesis, which means switching the order of sounds rather than adding a sound.

epenthesis.etymology: Middle of 16th century: via Late Latin, from Ancient Greek *ἐπένθεσις*, from *ἐπεντίθημι* (“to insert”), from *ἐπί* + *ἐντίθημι* (“to put in”), from *ἐν* (“in”) + *τίθημι* (“to put, place”).

senses.definition: A person, especially a philosopher, who studies theory of knowledge.

core.definition: A philosopher or scholar who studies epistemology, the theory of knowledge.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MAH, the vowel of cot. The -ology part reduces to luh-jist, so avoid stressing the -ol- or saying the g as a hard sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a professional specialty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word for philosophers who specialize in the theory of knowledge, mainly in academic settings. In everyday talk people usually say a philosopher who studies knowledge. Because the word is specialized, it is often explained when used in mixed company, and it is easy to confuse with epidemiologist.

distinctions.note: Philosopher is the broad term, while epistemologist names a specialist in the theory of knowledge.
A scientist studies the natural world, while an epistemologist studies how knowledge itself is justified.
A logician studies valid inference and formal reasoning, while an epistemologist studies the nature and limits of knowledge.

examples.everyday: My cousin is an epistemologist, so every family dinner turns into a debate about how we know what we know.
examples.professional: We hired an epistemologist on the AI ethics team to help define what counts as adequate evidence for a model's claims.
examples.analytical: Many contemporary epistemologists treat knowledge as justified true belief, though Gettier's counterexamples forced them to add further conditions.

nuance.analogy: Like an engineer who studies the design of a bridge rather than the traffic that crosses it.
nuance.etymology: From epistemology, from Greek epistēmē ('knowledge') and logos ('study, account'), plus the suffix -ist.
common_mistakes: Confusing epistemologist with epidemiologist, a specialist in disease patterns.
Using it for any expert in knowledge, when it specifically means a philosopher of knowledge.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in ih-pis-TUH-mo-lo-jist.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or being the person or entity after which someone or something is named; serving as an eponym.
senses.example: Prince Hamlet is the eponymous protagonist of the Shakespearian tragedy Hamlet.

senses.definition: Of a thing: named after a person or entity.
senses.example: The American singer-songwriter Madonna released her eponymous album in 1983.

core.definition: Given the name of a person, or being the person after whom something is named, as in "the eponymous hero" of a novel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, "PAH," and reduce the first and last vowels to a quick "uh." Many learners wrongly stress the first syllable or pronounce the final "ous" as a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a relationship between a name and a person or work, with no positive or negative judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use eponymous in book reviews, film criticism, and academic writing. A review might say "the eponymous hero of the novel," meaning the character who has the same name as the title. In everyday speech, people would more often say "the one named after him" or simply "the title character."

distinctions.note: Titular describes a person who holds a title in name only; eponymous means the thing is named after the person.
Namesake is a noun for a person who shares a name; eponymous is an adjective for the thing that carries the name.

examples.everyday: We watched the movie about the detective, and the eponymous character is actually based on a real cop from Boston.
examples.professional: The eponymous company was founded by the two engineers, and their names are on the first patents.
examples.analytical: The eponymous protagonist of the novel becomes a symbol of the moral failures the author wants to expose.

nuance.analogy: An eponymous title is like a family name on a shop door: the shop carries the name of the person who founded it.
nuance.etymology: From eponym, from Greek eponymos, "named after," from epi, "upon," and onoma, "name."
common_mistakes: Using eponymous to mean "famous," which it does not mean.
Saying "eponimous" with a short vowel in the second syllable instead of the reduced "uh."

eponymous.etymology: From Ancient Greek *ἐπώνῠμος* (“concerning giving one’s name to something; named in a significant manner; surnamed”) + *-ous*.

senses.definition: Equipment.
senses.example: Our field team's equipping arrived late, delaying the whole mountain survey.

core.definition: The act of supplying people with the skills, tools, and knowledge they need to do something well.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first full syllable, KWIP. The final '-ing' is a short 'ing' sound, not a long 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it describes helping people grow and succeed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'equipping' mostly as a gerund in church, education, leadership, and training contexts, such as 'equipping parents' or 'equipping volunteers'. As a plain noun for physical gear, Americans say 'equipment'. In casual conversation, 'helping people get ready' or 'training' are more common.

distinctions.note: Training is a structured process with lessons and practice; equipping includes training but emphasizes giving people the tools and confidence to act.
Equipment means physical objects; equipping is the process of preparing a person or group, not the objects.

examples.everyday: My church is focused on equipping parents to talk with their kids about faith and tough questions.
examples.professional: Our onboarding program focuses on equipping new analysts with the SQL and statistics they need in their first month.
examples.analytical: Paul's account of the church treats the equipping of believers as the purpose of ministry, not merely its reward.

nuance.analogy: Equipping is like a coach preparing an athlete: the athlete keeps the skills, not just the uniform.
nuance.etymology: Present participle of 'equip', from French équiper, from Old Norse skipa, 'to man a ship'.
common_mistakes: Using 'equipping' for physical gear; say 'equipment'.
Confusing 'equipping' with 'equipment' when you want the process of preparing people; use 'equipping' for the act and 'equipment' for objects.
nuance.biblical_note: In the New Testament, the idea of equipping is expressed in Greek by katartismos (preparation, full training, making complete) and exērtismenos (equipped, thoroughly furnished). Ephesians 4:11-12 says that Christ gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers to equip the saints for the work of ministry, and 2 Timothy 3:16-17 describes Scripture as making the man of God complete and equipped for every good work. Both passages present equipping as the purpose of teaching and gifts, not only as a skill set.

senses.definition: One who composes essays; a writer of short compositions.
senses.example: She was an essayist whose frequent contributions to the editorial pages of major newspapers had a loyal following.

core.definition: A writer who composes essays, especially personal or critical essays on literature, society or ideas.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, ESS. Keep the middle ay as a clear diphthong, like the vowel in day, and end with a short ist.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes a skilled writer and suggests thoughtfulness, though it is not a grand title like novelist.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use essayist for writers known for essays, such as Montaigne, Emerson or Joan Didion, usually in book reviews or literature classes. It is a little formal, so in casual conversation people more often say 'she writes essays' or 'she's a writer.' A natural follow-up is 'Have you read her latest collection?'

distinctions.note: A columnist writes regular opinion pieces for a newspaper, usually on current events, while an essayist may write longer reflective pieces on any subject.
An author is anyone who writes books or other works, while essayist names someone known specifically for essays.
A journalist reports the news, while an essayist offers personal or critical reflection.

examples.everyday: My sister is a really good essayist, so I always read her magazine pieces.
examples.professional: We hired a freelance essayist to write the foreword for our annual report.
examples.analytical: As an essayist, Montaigne treats the self as the proper subject of philosophical reflection.

nuance.analogy: An essayist is like a guide on a walk who stops to point out interesting things along the path rather than rushing to one destination.
nuance.etymology: From essay, from Old French essai ('trial'), plus the suffix -ist, 'one who does'.
common_mistakes: Reducing the middle ay to a weak uh sound, saying 'ESS-uh-ist'; keep the clear ay vowel.
Using essayist for anyone who writes short posts or blogs; the word usually implies a recognized essay writer.

senses.definition: Worthy of esteem; esteemed or estimable.

core.definition: Deserving of respect and admiration; worthy of being esteemed.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'STEEM', the same syllable as 'esteem'. Don't use the 'EH' stress of 'estimable', and reduce the ending to 'uh-bul'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises a person's character, though it is less warm and direct than 'admirable'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'esteemable' in conversation; they prefer 'admirable', 'respectable' or 'good'. It appears more often in formal writing, letters of recommendation, or speeches about someone's character. Calling a colleague 'esteemable' in a meeting would sound stiff but not rude.

distinctions.note: Estimable also means worthy of respect and is more common in writing; esteemable is rarer and sounds more deliberately formal.
Admirable stresses that a quality or action draws admiration; esteemable stresses the steady respect a person earns through character.
Respectable can describe a decent social standing or a moderate quality; esteemable suggests a higher, more personal regard.

examples.professional: Her esteemable work on the review board earned her a well-deserved promotion.
examples.analytical: A person can be esteemable without being admired, since esteem attaches to character rather than talent or fame.

nuance.analogy: If admiration is a bright spotlight on a performance, esteem is the steady warmth you feel toward someone who is reliably good.
nuance.etymology: From 'esteem' (from Old French estimer, from Latin aestimare) plus the suffix '-able'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'estimable' with stress on the first syllable.
Using it in casual speech where 'admirable' or 'respectable' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: The scientific study of animalian behavior, especially that of nonhuman animals.

core.definition: The scientific study of animal behavior, especially how animals behave in their natural environments and how that behavior evolved.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on THAH, the second syllable, and the middle syllables are reduced to a quick 'luh'. The final sound is a soft 'jee', not 'ji' as in 'gee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a scientific term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ethology' mainly in biology, zoology, and psychology courses or research writing. In everyday speech people usually say 'animal behavior'. Ethologists often focus on natural settings and instinct, rather than laboratory experiments.

distinctions.note: Behaviorism studies learned responses in controlled settings, while ethology emphasizes instinct and behavior in natural environments.
Zoology is the broad study of animals, while ethology is the narrower study of their behavior.

examples.everyday: My biology teacher said ethology is the study of why animals do what they do, like birds migrating.
examples.professional: Our research group uses ethology methods to observe wild primate behavior before modeling it with sensor data.
examples.analytical: Ethology asks whether a behavior is adaptive and how it evolved, which makes it distinct from purely mechanistic accounts of animal action.

nuance.analogy: Ethology is like watching a family in its own home rather than a lab, to understand what they do naturally.
nuance.etymology: From Greek ethos (habit, character) and -logy (study of).
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in 'ETH-ol-oh-jee'.
Confusing ethology with etiology or ethics, which are different fields.

ethology.etymology: From the Latin *ēthologia* (“the art of depicting or imitating character”), from the Ancient Greek *ἠθολογία* (“painting of character, especially by mimic gestures”), from *ἠθολόγος* (“painting character by mimic gestures”), from *ἦθος* (“character,…

senses.definition: To transition from a liquid state into a gaseous state.
senses.example: Water on the sidewalk began to evaporate as the morning sun warmed it.

senses.definition: To expel moisture from (usually by means of artificial heat), leaving the solid portion.
senses.example: to evaporate apples

senses.definition: To give vent to; to dissipate.
senses.example: Once he vented to his brother, his frustration seemed to evaporate.

senses.definition: To disappear; to escape or pass off without effect.
senses.example: The hopes we had for an easy fix quickly evaporated after the first failed test.

senses.definition: To cause to disappear or to escape or pass off without effect.
senses.example: The manager tried to evaporate the rumors by releasing the real schedule.

core.definition: To turn from a liquid into a vapor or gas, or to disappear gradually, as hopes or feelings do.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on VAP, the first syllable of the root. The middle 'o' reduces to a weak 'uh' sound, and the r is clearly pronounced in American speech. The final '-ate' is 'ayt'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical use. In figurative use it can suggest disappointment, as when hopes evaporate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'evaporate' for water in cooking, weather, and science, and they often use it figuratively for hopes, feelings, or a crowd that quickly vanishes. In everyday speech, saying 'the water evaporated' is natural, but saying 'the water evaporated quickly into the air' may sound repetitive. A casual alternative is 'disappear'.

distinctions.note: Vaporize means to turn into vapor, often by heating or by force, and it can happen quickly. Evaporate usually describes a gradual change at the surface of a liquid.
Dissipate means to scatter or fade gradually, as with fog, energy, or tension. It is more formal and does not necessarily involve a liquid turning into gas.

examples.everyday: Leave the pot on low for a few more minutes so the extra water can evaporate and the sauce thickens.
examples.professional: Our hopes that the vendor would deliver on time evaporated when they missed the second milestone.
examples.analytical: Such certainty evaporates under the pressure of a single counterexample, which is why careful philosophers hold their claims tentatively.

nuance.analogy: Evaporating is like morning dew disappearing from the grass as the sun warms it: the liquid slips into the air until nothing is left.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'evaporare', meaning to disperse as vapor, from 'e-' (out) and 'vapor' (steam, vapor).
common_mistakes: Confusing 'evaporate' with 'vaporize' when a gradual surface change is meant
Pronouncing the final '-ate' as 'it' rather than 'ayt'
Using 'evaporate' for solid objects, which do not evaporate

evaporate.etymology: Latin *ēvapōrātus*, the perfect passive participle of *ēvapōrō* (“to evaporate”), see *-ate* and *-ate*.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to high levels of activity; having many memorable events.
senses.example: With the number of drunken revellers on the streets it could hardly fail to be an eventful night.

core.definition: Full of exciting or important things happening; a day or period with many notable events.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, VENT, not on the first. Don't add a vowel between the n and the t; say it as one quick consonant cluster, ending in a soft ful.

nuance.connotation: Usually neutral to positive, meaning busy or interesting. It can be negative when the events are bad, as in an eventful trip that went wrong.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use eventful for days, trips, meetings, or lives that had a lot happening, often with humor or understatement. Saying your weekend was eventful usually invites a question about what happened. Many people also use it to mean chaotic or stressful, depending on tone.

distinctions.note: Busy describes a schedule full of tasks, while eventful describes a period with notable happenings.
Exciting describes the feeling an experience creates, while eventful only says many things happened.

examples.everyday: How was your trip to Denver? Oh, it was eventful. Our flight got delayed twice.
examples.professional: The quarter was eventful for the team, with two product launches and a major client renewal.
examples.analytical: Historians often describe a century as eventful when it contains many decisive ruptures, yet the word tells us little about the structures that shaped those events.

nuance.analogy: An eventful day is like a crowded calendar where every hour has something written in it.
nuance.etymology: From event, from Latin eventus, outcome, plus the suffix -ful.
common_mistakes: Using eventful for a single event; it describes a period or experience with many events, so say an eventful day, not an eventful party when you mean one party.
Stressing the first syllable in the wrong place by saying ih-VEN-tful with the stress on the middle.

senses.definition: The act of evicting.
senses.example: order of eviction

senses.definition: The state of being evicted.

core.definition: The legal process or act of forcing a tenant or occupant to leave a property, or in computing, removing data from memory.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on VIK, and the -tion ending is pronounced shun, not tee-on. The first syllable is reduced to a short ih.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It refers to a serious loss of housing in housing contexts, and a neutral technical event in computing.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, eviction refers to the legal removal of a tenant, and it is often discussed in news about housing costs. In data science and software engineering, it means removing items from a cache or memory. Say the eviction process for the legal sense, and cache eviction for the technical one.

distinctions.note: Removal is broad and neutral, while eviction is a legal or technical removal from a specific place or memory.
Foreclosure is about losing property because of unpaid loans, while eviction is about losing a rented home.

examples.everyday: After the rent went up again, several families in our building were facing eviction.
examples.professional: We need a cache eviction policy that removes the least recently used entries when the memory limit is reached.
examples.analytical: The sociology of eviction shows how housing insecurity produces long-term harm beyond the loss of a single home.

nuance.analogy: An eviction in a cache is like clearing the oldest dishes from a crowded sink so that new ones have room.
nuance.etymology: From evict, from Latin evincere, to overcome, with the noun suffix -ion.
common_mistakes: Confusing eviction with foreclosure, which applies to owners who lose property due to unpaid mortgages.
Using eviction for a person leaving voluntarily; the word implies the process was forced.

eviction.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *éviction*, from Late Latin *ēvictiō*, from Latin *ēvincō*.

senses.definition: To overstate, to describe more than the fact.
senses.example: I've told you a billion times not to exaggerate!

senses.definition: Exaggerative; overblown.
senses.example: His exaggerated claims about the project made the review board skeptical.

core.definition: To describe something as bigger, better, worse, or more than it really is.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on ZAJ, the first full syllable. The middle syllable is reduced to a quick 'er' sound, so don't say 'ex-ag-ger-ate' with equal stress.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies that the speaker is distorting the truth, although it can be playful when the distortion is obvious.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word constantly in everyday talk, often with 'a little' or 'a lot' in front. Saying 'Don't exaggerate' is a common, mild way to tell someone to be realistic. In a friendly setting you can say 'I'm not exaggerating' to stress that you are telling the truth.

distinctions.note: A lie is a deliberate falsehood; exaggerating starts from something partly true and inflates it.
Overstate is more formal and used in reports and arguments; exaggerate is the everyday word.

examples.everyday: My brother always exaggerates how far he ran, so I'd take his story with a grain of salt.
examples.professional: Please don't exaggerate the model's accuracy in the slides; we only tested it on one dataset.
examples.analytical: The critic argues that the author exaggerates the role of chance in order to strengthen his claim about providence.

nuance.analogy: Like a funhouse mirror that makes a small thing look huge, exaggeration stretches the truth until the shape is distorted.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exaggeratus, past participle of exaggerare 'to heap up', from ex- plus agger 'heap, mound'.
common_mistakes: Using 'exaggerate' as a noun; the noun is exaggeration.
Stressing the last syllable (-ATE) instead of the first.

exaggerate.etymology: Latin *exaggerātus*, perfect passive participle of *exaggerō* (“to heap up, increase, enlarge, magnify, amplify, exaggerate”) (see *-ate* and *-ate*), from *ex-* (“out, up”) + *aggerō* (“to heap up”), from *agger* (“a pile, heap, mound, dike, mole, pier,…

senses.definition: To surpass someone or something; to be better or do better than someone or something.
senses.example: I excelled everyone else with my exam results.

senses.definition: To do much better than usual.
senses.example: Everyone agreed Magnus really excelled himself this tournament.

senses.definition: To be much better than others.

core.definition: To be very good at something, or to do something much better than most other people.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second and only stressed syllable, 'sel,' with a short 'e' like 'bed.' Do not add an extra syllable or say 'ex-sell' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it praises skill or performance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say excel to praise someone who is strong at a task, school subject, or sport, as in 'She excels at math.' It is common in school, work, and sports talk. In casual speech people often prefer 'be really good at,' but excel is natural in reviews, recommendations, and news reports.

distinctions.note: Succeed means to achieve a goal, while excel means to perform unusually well in a skill or area.
Surpass means to go beyond someone else's achievement, while excel describes outstanding performance in itself.

examples.everyday: My daughter really excels at soccer, so we go to every game.
examples.professional: Maria excels in client presentations, so she should lead the next review.
examples.analytical: Aristotle held that a thing excels when it fully performs the function proper to its kind.

nuance.analogy: Like a runner who pulls ahead of the pack and keeps going.
nuance.etymology: From Latin excellere, 'to rise up, surpass,' from ex- 'out' and -cellere 'to rise.'
common_mistakes: Using the wrong preposition: say 'excel at' or 'excel in,' not 'excel on.'
Confusing 'excel' with 'exceed' in the sense of going beyond a limit.
nuance.biblical_note: The English verb 'excel' is not a distinct term in the Greek New Testament, but Scripture repeatedly speaks of excelling in faith, love, and gifts. Paul urges believers to abound in such graces, as in 1 Corinthians 12:31, where he tells them to strive for the greater gifts, and in 1 Corinthians 13, where love is presented as the greatest of all.

senses.definition: In an excited manner.

core.definition: In an eager, enthusiastic or emotionally aroused way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, SY. The middle syllable is a quick, reduced vowel, so the -ed sounds like a short id, and the word ends in lee.

nuance.connotation: Positive, showing eagerness or happiness; it can also suggest nervous energy, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use excitedly to describe how someone speaks, moves or reacts, as in 'She waved excitedly at the parade.' It is neutral in tone and works in casual speech and writing. In everyday talk, people often say 'I'm so excited' rather than using the adverb.

distinctions.note: Eagerly stresses wanting something and looking forward to it; excitedly stresses visible emotional energy in the moment.
Enthusiastically is more formal and suggests sustained interest or support, often at work or in a group.

examples.everyday: My daughter ran to the door and waved excitedly at the mail carrier.
examples.professional: The product team talked excitedly about the new dashboard during Monday's standup.
examples.analytical: Early reformers wrote excitedly about a new age of reason, yet their optimism often hid unexamined assumptions.

nuance.analogy: Like a dog's tail wagging fast when its owner comes home: the feeling shows in the movement.
nuance.etymology: Formed from excited, the past participle of excite, plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using the adjective instead of the adverb: say 'She spoke excitedly', not 'She spoke excited'.
Pronouncing the -ed ending as a full ed sound instead of a short id sound.

senses.definition: The act of enlivening the spirits; the act of making glad or cheerful; a gladdening.
senses.example: The exhilaration of the first snowfall lifted the whole neighborhood's spirits that morning.

senses.definition: The state of being enlivened, cheerful or exhilarated.

core.definition: A strong feeling of happiness, energy and excitement, often from a thrilling experience or achievement.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the -ray- syllable, and the -tion ending is pronounced 'shun' with a reduced vowel. The 'ur' in the third syllable is an American r-colored vowel, so do not pronounce a full 'a'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It names an intense, joyful feeling, often mixed with a sense of energy or freedom.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exhilaration for big highs: crossing a finish line, a first flight, or a sudden success at work. It is a bit more elevated than 'excitement' and often appears in writing, interviews and descriptions. In casual talk people usually say 'what a rush' or 'so exciting', but 'exhilaration' is natural when describing a memorable moment.

distinctions.note: Excitement is broader and can refer to anticipation, while exhilaration is a more intense sense of being lifted up in the moment.
Elation is a feeling of great joy and pride, often after good news, while exhilaration includes a physical sense of energy and speed.

examples.everyday: When the plane lifted off, I felt a rush of exhilaration I still remember.
examples.professional: There was real exhilaration in the room when the launch metrics came in above target.
examples.analytical: Descartes distinguishes passions of joy from mere bodily agitation, yet the exhilaration of discovery seems to blend both.

nuance.analogy: Exhilaration is like the fizz in sparkling water: it rises fast, feels bright, and is strongest at the top.
nuance.etymology: From exhilarate, from Latin exhilarare 'to make cheerful'.
common_mistakes: Using 'exhilaration' as a verb, as in 'it exhilaration me'; the verb is 'exhilarate'.
Pronouncing the middle as 'hil-AIR' with a strong second stress instead of the reduced 'zil-uh'.

senses.definition: Existing; having life or being, current; occurring now.

core.definition: Currently existing or present; actually in being rather than merely imagined or possible.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, ZIST. The ending -ent is reduced to a light schwa sound, so it sounds like ig-ZIS-tuhnt.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a precise philosophical or technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use existent mainly in philosophy, logic, or formal writing, where it contrasts with merely possible or imagined things. In everyday speech, people say existing or real. Using existent in casual conversation would sound stiff.

distinctions.note: Existing is the everyday word for something that is there now; existent is more formal and is used in philosophical or logical contexts.
Extant means still surviving, often said of old manuscripts or species; existent means currently existing in general.

examples.everyday: Some people think unicorns are existent, but I've never seen one, so I'm not convinced.
examples.professional: Before we build the feature, we need to confirm that the data source is existent and still being updated.
examples.analytical: Aquinas distinguishes between what is merely possible and what is actually existent, and this distinction shapes his metaphysics.

nuance.analogy: An existent thing is like a chair in the room, as opposed to a chair you only imagine sitting in.
nuance.etymology: From Latin existens, present participle of existere, to exist, from ex- out plus sistere, to stand.
common_mistakes: Using existent in everyday speech where existing is more natural.
Confusing existent with extant when describing surviving documents.
patterns: existent (usually after a noun or verb)

senses.definition: To consume, exhaust.
senses.example: The marathon runner expended almost all of her energy in the final two miles.

core.definition: To spend or use up money, time, energy, or effort on something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the single syllable, spend. The final d is pronounced clearly, and the first vowel is short and reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use expend mostly in formal, business, or technical writing, such as energy or resources expended on a project. In everyday talk they say spend, use, or put in. Using expend in casual conversation sounds stiff, though it is natural in reports.

distinctions.note: Spend is the everyday word for money or time, while expend is more formal and often used for energy, effort, or resources.
Consume means to use up completely, often in a process like eating or burning fuel, while expend emphasizes deliberate use of resources.

examples.everyday: I don't want to expend any more energy on this argument, so let's just order dinner.
examples.professional: We should expend our limited engineering time on the features that customers request most often.
examples.analytical: A theory of virtue must explain why people expend effort on others when no direct reward is available.

nuance.analogy: To expend resources is like drawing from a bank account: each withdrawal reduces what remains until nothing is left.
nuance.etymology: From Latin expendere, "to weigh out, pay out," from ex- and pendere, "to weigh."
common_mistakes: Using expend for everyday money spending; spend is the natural choice.
Using expend with a direct object of a person, as in expend someone; it applies to resources, effort, or time.

expend.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *expendō* (“to weigh; to pay out”).

senses.definition: An algorithm whose running time increases as an exponential function of the size of its input.

core.definition: In computer science, the running time of an algorithm that grows as an exponential function of the size of its input.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on NEN in exponential and on TYME in time. The first syllable of exponential is a reduced schwa, so say 'ek-spuh' rather than 'ex-poh.'

nuance.connotation: Negative in computing, because it means an algorithm becomes impractical as the input grows.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exponential time mainly in computer science, algorithm analysis, and software engineering. It is almost always used when comparing algorithms, often alongside polynomial time. Outside technical settings it sounds unusual, so people usually say 'really slow' instead.

distinctions.note: Polynomial time grows as a power of the input size, so it is usually practical. Exponential time grows so fast that only small inputs can be solved.
Linear time grows in direct proportion to the input size. Exponential time grows much faster and quickly becomes infeasible.

examples.everyday: My friend joked that his sorting code runs in exponential time, so he never tries it on big lists.
examples.professional: A brute-force search of every password combination takes exponential time, which is why longer passwords are safer.
examples.analytical: A problem that can be solved only in exponential time, and not in polynomial time, is not known to belong to the class P.

nuance.analogy: An algorithm running in exponential time is like a lock where each extra digit doubles the number of combinations you have to try: a few digits are easy, but thirty digits are hopeless.
nuance.etymology: Exponential comes from Latin exponere 'set forth'; time is from Old English tima.
common_mistakes: Using exponential time to mean any slow process; in computing it has a precise definition about input size.
Saying 'EX-po-nen-shul' with a strong first syllable; the stress is on NEN.

senses.definition: In an extemporaneous manner; without prior preparation or planning.
senses.example: Considering that he was speaking extemporaneously, he covered the subject pretty well.

core.definition: In a way done without written notes or prior preparation, speaking or performing spontaneously on the spot.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on RAY, with a light secondary stress on the first syllable. Many learners stress the first syllable or say the middle vowels too strongly, but the -pore- part reduces to uh, and the r is flapped and rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes how something was delivered and carries a sense of skill or confidence when done well.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use extemporaneously mainly in public speaking, debate, academic talks, and formal presentations, often in phrases like 'speaking extemporaneously.' In everyday talk people more often say off the cuff, ad-lib, or without notes. Speech and debate coaches use it often, so it is a useful word for work settings.

distinctions.note: Impromptu means unplanned and sudden, while extemporaneously means spoken from knowledge without a script, even if the topic was known in advance.
Ad lib is more informal and often used for entertainment or jokes, while extemporaneously sounds more formal and suits speeches and presentations.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor is so good at talking to the city council that she can speak extemporaneously for ten minutes.
examples.professional: Please present the quarterly results extemporaneously, but keep the slides as a backup in case the projector fails.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's rhetoric assumes that a speaker who argues extemporaneously must still draw on well-ordered knowledge.

nuance.analogy: Like a jazz musician who plays a solo from memory of the chords, not from sheet music.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ex tempore, 'on the spur of the moment', from ex 'from' plus tempore, the ablative of tempus 'time'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (EKS-tem-puh-ray-nee-us-lee) instead of the RAY syllable.
Using extemporaneously to mean hastily or carelessly; it implies skill and knowledge, not carelessness.
