senses.definition: A video game designed to convey a more or less realistic experience, as of a sport or warfare.
senses.example: Some kids in the classroom will be playing simulations after school.

senses.definition: Assuming an appearance which is feigned, or not true.
senses.example: His sudden illness was a simulation meant to avoid the difficult exam.

senses.definition: The act of falling over in order to be awarded a foul, when no foul has been committed.
senses.example: The referee was furious at the simulation, since the striker had clearly dived inside the box.

core.definition: A computer or physical model that imitates a real system or environment to predict how it will behave.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LAY. The ending -tion is pronounced 'shun', and the final syllable has no separate vowel. Non-native speakers often stress the first syllable instead.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In everyday talk it can mean a video game or a training exercise, and in technical talk it means a computed model.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use simulation for flight training, Monte Carlo runs and racing games. In data and engineering work, a simulation is a run of a model over many scenarios. In casual conversation, people often use it for a driving or racing video game.

distinctions.note: A model is the mathematical or physical structure; a simulation is running that model over time to see what happens.
Emulation copies the behavior of another system, often on different hardware; simulation predicts the behavior of a real-world system.
A prediction is a single expected outcome; a simulation is a tool that generates many possible outcomes.

examples.everyday: My son spends hours on a racing simulation game.
examples.professional: Let's run a simulation of the new pricing model before we commit to it.
examples.analytical: A simulation can reproduce a pattern without explaining why it occurs, which is a real limit of the method.

nuance.analogy: A simulation is like a wind tunnel for ideas: you test a design against imagined weather before you build it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin simulatio, from simulare, to imitate.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as SIM-yoo-lay-shun.
Using simulation for a video game in professional writing without context; in data work it means a computed model.

simulation.etymology: First attested in 1340 as Middle English *symulacioun*, from Middle French *simulation*, from Old French *simulation*/*simulacion*, from Latin *simulātiōnem*, from *simulō* (“imitate”).

conversation.text: Training in simulation is cheap and safe, but the robot still has to work in the real world.
We built a simulation of the support desk so the agent can practice on synthetic customers.
The flight simulation felt surprisingly real.

core.definition: The mountain in the Sinai wilderness where God gave Moses the Law and made the covenant with Israel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SY, and the final -ai is pronounced 'eye'. Avoid saying it as sin-AY or sigh-NAY.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a place name, though it carries strong religious significance in Judaism and Christianity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Sinai in Bible study, history and news about Egypt. Mount Sinai names the mountain, while the Sinai Peninsula names the region in Egypt. In theology, phrases like the Sinai covenant are common.

distinctions.note: Horeb is another name for the mountain of the Law in Deuteronomy; Sinai is the usual name in Exodus.
The Sinai Peninsula is a modern region of Egypt, while Mount Sinai is a specific mountain within the biblical story.

collocations: the Ten Commandments given at Sinai

examples.everyday: We visited a church named after Mount Sinai when we went to Egypt.
examples.professional: The sermon series connected the Exodus narrative with the covenant given at Sinai.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the traditional site of Sinai in the southern peninsula is the original location of the covenant.

nuance.analogy: Sinai is like the place where the rules of a nation were first written down and signed.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; no firm etymology is established.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in sigh-NAY.
Confusing Mount Sinai with the Sinai Peninsula, which is a larger region in Egypt.
nuance.biblical_note: Sinai is where Moses received the Law. Exodus 19 describes God descending on the mountain, and Exodus 20 gives the Ten Commandments. Exodus 34:29 describes Moses coming down from the mountain with his face shining after speaking with God. Galatians 4:24-25 uses Mount Sinai allegorically, linking it with the covenant of bondage.

senses.definition: NATO & ICAO radiotelephony clear code (spelling-alphabet name) for the digit 6.
A group or set with six elements.
The digit or figure 6.
A playing card featuring six pips.
A person who is six years old.
senses.example: The fives and sixes will have a snack first, then the older kids.

senses.definition: Six o'clock.
Rear, behind (rear side of something).
senses.example: cover my six

senses.definition: A touchdown.
Small beer sold at six shillings per barrel.
An event whereby a batsman hits a ball which does not bounce before passing over a boundary in the air, resulting in an award of 6 runs for the batting team.
senses.example: His century featured 12 sixes.

core.definition: The number 6, which comes after five and before seven.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short 'i' and end with a sharp 'ks' cluster; don't add a vowel after the s. Avoid making it sound like 'sex', which has a different vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a basic number with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use six for times ('six o'clock'), ages, prices, and quantities. For phone numbers and some digit strings, speakers often read each digit separately. In casual talk, 'half past six' or '6:30' are both common.

distinctions.note: Six is a cardinal number used for counting; sixth is an ordinal used for position, as in the sixth floor.
Six has a short 'i' vowel and sex has a short 'e' vowel; the difference is important in conversation.

examples.everyday: We'll be there at six, so save us a table if you can.
examples.professional: The release is six weeks out, so we need the final review by Thursday.
examples.analytical: Six is the first perfect number, since it equals the sum of its proper divisors, one, two, and three.

nuance.analogy: Six is one more than five and one less than seven, like a middle step on a staircase.
nuance.etymology: From Old English siex, from Proto-Germanic *sehs, related to Latin sex.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing six as 'sicks' with a short vowel that is too long, or 'siks' with a vowel that sounds like 'sex'.
Using six where sixth is needed, as in 'the six floor' instead of 'the sixth floor'.

six.etymology: From Middle English *six*, from Old English *six*, from **sehs*, from Proto-Germanic **sehs*, from Proto-Indo-European **swéḱs*.

senses.definition: The ordinal form of the number six.
The person or thing in the sixth position.
senses.example: She finished sixth in the marathon, just missing a podium spot by seconds.

senses.definition: One of six equal parts of a whole.
senses.example: Mix one sixth of the flour with butter before adding the remaining ingredients.

senses.definition: The interval between one note and another, five notes higher in the scale; for example C to A, a major sixth, or C to A flat, a minor sixth.
senses.example: The jazz pianist played a rich sixth above the melody in every chorus.

core.definition: Coming in position number six in a series; the ordinal form of six, written 6th.

pronunciation.tip: End with 'ks' and then the unvoiced 'th' with the tongue tip between the teeth. Many learners drop the final t or insert an extra vowel, so keep the cluster tight.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a simple ordinal used for position or order.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sixth for floors, grades, birthdays, and items in lists. In school, 'sixth grade' is common, and in music 'sixth' names an interval. 'The sixth sense' is a common idiom for intuition.

distinctions.note: Sixth is an ordinal used for position; sixty is a cardinal number meaning six tens, and the two are easily confused in speech.
Six counts how many; sixth tells which one in order.

examples.everyday: We live on the sixth floor, so the elevator is a lifesaver after groceries.
examples.professional: The sixth item on today's agenda is the vendor contract, so let's save it for last.
examples.analytical: Her sixth premise, that the sample is independent, is the weakest assumption in the whole argument.

nuance.analogy: Sixth is like the sixth stop on a train route: you have passed five others before reaching it.
nuance.etymology: Formed from six plus the ordinal suffix -th, from Old English.
common_mistakes: Dropping the final t and saying 'siks' instead of 'siksth'.
Confusing sixth with sixty in speech, especially in numbers like 'sixth' and 'sixty' in dates.

sixth.etymology: From earlier *sixt*, from Middle English *sixte*, from Old English *siexta*, from Proto-Germanic **sehstô*.

senses.definition: A measure of the asymmetry of the probability distribution of a real-valued random variable; is the third standardized moment, defined as γ1=μ3σ3, where μ3 is the third moment about the mean and σ is the standard deviation.
senses.example: The income data showed strong positive skewness, so the mean overstated typical household earnings.

senses.definition: The property of being skew.
senses.example: The bridge's skewness made the approach look crooked from the north side.

core.definition: A measure of how asymmetric a probability distribution is; positive skew means a longer right tail, negative skew a longer left tail.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the 'ew' in 'skew' is a long oo sound, so say SKYOO, not SKOO. The final -ness is a reduced, unstressed 'nus'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Used almost only in statistics, data science and quantitative research, where it is a precise technical term. Analysts often say 'the data is right-skewed' or 'skewness is positive' when describing a distribution. Outside technical settings, Americans would say 'lopsidedness' or 'asymmetry' instead.

distinctions.note: Skewness measures asymmetry (lean left or right), while kurtosis measures how heavy the tails are and how peaked the distribution is.
Asymmetry is the general idea of lacking symmetry; skewness is the specific third-moment measure of it for a distribution.

examples.everyday: My commute times are really skewed by a few terrible days when the highway closes.
examples.professional: The revenue data has strong positive skewness, so I'll use the median instead of the mean in the dashboard.
examples.analytical: A distribution with zero skewness is symmetric about its mean, though zero skewness alone does not guarantee a normal distribution.

nuance.analogy: Skewness is like a mountain range that leans to one side: the slope is gentle on one side and steep on the other.
nuance.etymology: From 'skew', probably from Old Norse or Middle English roots meaning oblique or slanting, with the -ness noun suffix added.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'ew' as a short vowel, as in 'skuh-NESS'.
Confusing skewness with kurtosis, which is a different shape measure.

senses.definition: The thin board used in skimboarding.
To take part in skimboarding.

core.definition: A thin, flat board that riders run onto and slide across on a thin sheet of shallow water on a beach.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. In 'board' the r is clearly pronounced in American speech, so say it with a firm r, not 'bore-d' with no r. Keep 'skim' short and do not say 'skeem'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names equipment and a beach sport, mostly used by surfers and beachgoers.
nuance.usage_note: Skimboarding is popular on beaches in California and Florida, where people run and throw a small board onto the thin wash of a wave. Do not confuse a skimboard with a surfboard, which is much longer and is ridden on waves in the ocean. Americans say 'skimboard' for the equipment and 'skimboarding' for the sport.

distinctions.note: A surfboard is long and ridden on ocean waves, while a skimboard is short and used on a thin layer of shallow water.
A bodyboard is ridden lying down or kneeling on waves, while a skimboard is ridden standing up on a thin wash of water.

examples.everyday: My son got a new skimboard for his birthday, so we're going to the beach this weekend.
examples.professional: Our outdoor sports marketing team is launching a campaign for the new skimboard line in coastal stores.
examples.analytical: Skimboarding grew out of informal play on California beaches, showing how a simple board can build a distinct sport culture.

nuance.analogy: A skimboard is like a flat stone skipping over the water, except that a rider stands on it.
nuance.etymology: From skim, from Middle English skimmen, plus board, from Old English bord.
common_mistakes: Thinking a skimboard is the same as a surfboard; they are different boards for different waters
Saying 'skim-BOARD' with stress on the second syllable
Writing 'skim board' as two words; the standard form is one word, 'skimboard'

senses.definition: Shallow, superficial.

core.definition: Superficial; affecting only the outward appearance rather than deeper character or real qualities.

pronunciation.tip: Put the main stress on DEEP, the second word. The first word gets a weaker secondary stress. Link the two words smoothly, with a clear n before the d.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It usually criticizes something shallow, though it can describe a minor surface problem without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'skin-deep' in the saying 'Beauty is only skin-deep', meaning appearances do not show a person's character. It can come before a noun, as in a skin-deep change, or after a verb with 'only', as in the change was only skin-deep. A natural reply is 'Exactly, character matters more' or 'Yeah, looks fade and character lasts.'

distinctions.note: Superficial is a more formal, general word for anything shallow; skin-deep is more vivid and often used about beauty or appearance.
Shallow can describe a person's character or the depth of water; skin-deep focuses on outward looks or change.
Cosmetic means affecting only appearance in a physical or product sense; skin-deep is more figurative and often judges character.

examples.everyday: People say beauty is only skin-deep, but I think kindness shows up over time.
examples.professional: The redesign was only skin-deep, because we changed the colors but left the slow checkout process untouched.
examples.analytical: A moral reform that changes only behavior and never the heart is skin-deep, and Scripture repeatedly challenges such outward conformity.

nuance.analogy: A skin-deep fix is like painting over rust: it looks new, but the metal underneath keeps corroding.
nuance.etymology: From skin (from Old Norse skinn) and deep (from Old English deop).
common_mistakes: Writing skin deep without a hyphen when it comes before a noun
Using it for physical depth, such as a cut, rather than shallow appearance or character
Putting the main stress on SKIN instead of on DEEP

senses.definition: The state of being slack; the quality of having slack.
Vulgarity in West Indian culture.
senses.example: Critics of the performance complained that its slackness had gone too far for family audiences.

senses.definition: A subgenre of dancehall music with sexual lyrics.
senses.example: The DJ's set was pure slackness, with lyrics that drew loud laughs from the crowd.

core.definition: The condition of being loose rather than tight, or lacking firmness, tension, or activity.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SLAK. The final syllable is weak, so say 'nus' with a reduced vowel, not 'ness' with a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical contexts; negative when it describes lax standards, weak discipline, or slow business.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use slackness mostly in technical or descriptive writing about ropes, belts, cables, or markets, and when discussing weak discipline. In everyday speech they usually say 'looseness' or 'slack'. The Caribbean and dancehall senses in some dictionaries are not part of general American English.

distinctions.note: Looseness is the everyday word for something not held tight; slackness is more technical or descriptive.
Laxity usually means lax enforcement of rules or standards; slackness can be physical or general.

examples.everyday: There's some slackness in the hammock, so tighten the ropes a bit.
examples.professional: The slackness in demand this quarter means we should slow the hiring.
examples.analytical: The slackness of the argument lies in its refusal to define its key terms.

nuance.analogy: Like a clothesline sagging between two posts.
nuance.etymology: From slack, plus the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ending as a full 'ness' vowel; the second syllable is weak.
Using slackness to mean a person's laziness; say laziness or slacking instead.

senses.definition: A thin strip of metal such as spring steel used to unlock automobile doors without a key.
Someone or something very thin.
A kind of dipole radio antenna.
senses.example: He mounted a slim jim antenna on the roof to improve his ham radio reception.

senses.definition: Very thin.
senses.example: He is so slim jim that his jacket hangs loosely.

core.definition: A thin strip of spring steel used to unlock a car door from inside without a key.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second word, JIM, with the first word lightly stressed. Both words have a short i, so say them quickly, as in slim and gym.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; in conversation it often signals car break-ins or locksmith talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use slim jim when talking about cars: a locked-out driver, a locksmith or police describing car break-ins may mention one. It is an informal tool name, and calling a person a slim jim as a joke is possible but unusual. When locked out, most Americans call a locksmith or roadside service rather than try a slim jim themselves.

distinctions.note: A lockpick works on a lock's internal pins, while a slim jim reaches the latch rod inside a car door.
A car key is the legitimate way to open the door, while a slim jim is an improvised tool for getting in without one.

collocations: locked out with a slim jim
car break-in with a slim jim

examples.everyday: The locksmith said he could open the car with a slim jim, but he'd rather call a service.
examples.professional: Our fleet manager said the thieves used a slim jim, so we added locks to the trucks.
examples.analytical: The slim jim is a simple tool, and its existence shows how a physical barrier often depends on hidden mechanisms.

nuance.analogy: Like a thin metal key that works by sliding into a mechanism instead of turning a lock's pins.
common_mistakes: Assuming slim jim is a person's name; in English it is usually a tool or a brand of meat snack.
Stressing both words equally; the stronger stress falls on JIM.

senses.definition: To shift chaotically; to splash noisily.
senses.example: The water in his bottle sloshed back and forth as he ran.

senses.definition: To cause to slosh.
senses.example: The boy sloshed water over the edge of the bath.

senses.definition: To make a sloshing sound.
senses.example: His boots were so completely soaked that they sloshed when he walked.

senses.definition: To pour noisily, sloppily or in large amounts.
senses.example: The coffee was nice and hot, so she sloshed some into a cup and went back to her desk.

senses.definition: To move noisily through water or other liquid.
senses.example: The streets were flooded, but they still managed to slosh their way to school.

senses.definition: A quantity of a liquid; more than a splash.
senses.example: We added a slosh of white wine to the sauce.

senses.definition: A sloshing sound or motion.
senses.example: I heard a slosh of water as the bucket tipped over on the porch.

senses.definition: Slush.
senses.example: Gray slosh covered the sidewalks after the snowstorm, so every crosswalk turned soggy and treacherous.

senses.definition: Inferior wine or other drink.
senses.example: The cheap house wine was pure slosh, and nobody at the party finished a second glass.

senses.definition: A game related to billiards.
senses.example: After dinner we played slosh on the old table in the basement, the rules scribbled on a napkin.

senses.definition: Backslash, the character \.
senses.example: When writing the file path in the script, remember to escape the slosh before each folder name.

core.definition: To move around noisily in a liquid, or to splash liquid about in a messy, sloshing way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the only syllable, and the vowel is the short open 'ah' of 'cot'. Don't add a 'w' sound or confuse it with 'slush', which has a 'uh' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a physical motion and carries little judgment, though it can suggest carelessness with liquids.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use slosh for liquid moving back and forth inside a container, such as coffee in a cup on a bumpy bus or water in a bucket being carried. It is casual and descriptive, and it is common in everyday speech. In a noun sense, a slosh is a small amount of liquid, as in 'a slosh of wine left in the glass'.

distinctions.note: Splash suggests a sudden spray of liquid, while slosh suggests liquid moving back and forth in a container.
Slop means liquid spilling messily over edges, often onto something, while slosh stresses the back-and-forth motion.

examples.everyday: Be careful with that bucket, you're going to slosh water all over the floor.
examples.professional: The sensor tanks sloshed during transport, so we added baffles to stabilize the readings.
examples.analytical: The poem's rhythm sloshes back and forth between stanzas, mirroring the restless grief of its speaker.

nuance.analogy: Like a bathtub when someone climbs in quickly, the liquid rocks back and forth in the container.
nuance.etymology: Probably imitative of the sound of liquid moving, related to slush.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the vowel like 'slaw' in 'slaw' or 'law', which makes it sound like a different word.
Confusing slosh with slush, which refers to partly melted snow or ice.

senses.definition: A boxer who tends to deliver hard punches.
senses.example: The slugger in the ring kept swinging for the body, hoping to wear down his opponent.

senses.definition: Buddy, dude, champ.
senses.example: Good to see you, slugger!

senses.definition: A batter who has a high percentage of extra base hits.
senses.example: That will bring up the slugger, Jones.

core.definition: A baseball batter who hits the ball hard and often, especially one who hits many home runs and extra-base hits.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable 'SLUG', and the second syllable is a weak, r-colored 'er'. Do not pronounce it as 'slug-gah' or add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises a player's power and is used with admiration in sports talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use slugger mostly in baseball, as in 'He's the team's best slugger.' In boxing, slugger means a fighter who punches hard, and it is less common today. Some dictionaries also list an informal sense used as a form of address, like 'buddy' or 'champ', but that use is uncommon in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: A hitter is any batter, while a slugger is specifically a batter known for power hitting and home runs.
Power hitter means the same as slugger in baseball, but slugger is more colorful and more common in sports writing.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor's kid is a real slugger in Little League, and he hits the ball over the fence.
examples.professional: Our top sales slugger closed more deals than anyone else last quarter.
examples.analytical: Baseball history celebrates the slugger, but the modern game also values on-base skill and defense.

nuance.analogy: Like the heavy hitter in a band of players, the one who brings the most power to every big moment.
nuance.etymology: From slug (to hit hard) plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using slugger for any strong or aggressive person in everyday talk, which can sound odd outside sports.
Confusing the baseball sense with the boxing sense, since context usually determines which is meant.

senses.definition: A person who accomplishes tasks with efficiency and grace, especially one with verbal skills who is persuasive in interpersonal relationships, negotiation, etc.
senses.example: Our new sales director is a real smooth operator, closing deals with a warm smile.

senses.definition: A skillful, manipulative person, con artist, or clever scoundrel.
senses.example: Don't trust that stranger; he's a smooth operator who empties wallets at county fairs.

core.definition: A person who handles people and tasks with ease and charm, often in a persuasive or sometimes slippery way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on AH in operator, while smooth has a lighter stress; the middle syllables of operator are reduced to a schwa and r. The t in operator is a flap, so it sounds like a quick d, and the final syllable is a reduced er sound.

nuance.connotation: Mixed. It is often positive when describing a skilled negotiator or host, but it can be negative when suggesting a manipulative or insincere person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use smooth operator in casual speech to praise someone who can handle difficult people or situations gracefully, or to describe a charming salesperson. The phrase can be a warning, suggesting that the person may be too slick or not fully trustworthy. A natural reply might be something like yeah, he's a real smooth operator.

distinctions.note: Slick is more often negative, implying a superficial or deceptive polish, while smooth operator can be admiring or teasing.
A charmer is pleasant and attractive to others, while a smooth operator focuses on getting results with skill, sometimes at the expense of candor.

examples.everyday: My neighbor Mike is a real smooth operator, because he can get a parking spot anywhere in the city.
examples.professional: We need a smooth operator on the account team who can calm frustrated clients without making promises we cannot keep.
examples.analytical: Describing a negotiator as a smooth operator reveals a tension between admiration for social skill and suspicion of a manipulative edge.

nuance.analogy: A smooth operator is like a skilled river guide who knows where the rocks are and steers you through without anyone noticing the effort.
common_mistakes: Stressing smooth and operator equally, when operator gets the main stress in the noun phrase.
Using smooth operator only for compliments, when it can also suggest a manipulative or untrustworthy person.

senses.definition: To be devious and cunning so as not to be seen.
senses.example: The thief learned to snoop past the guards by hiding in the shadows.

senses.definition: To secretly spy on or investigate, especially into the private personal life of others.
senses.example: If I had not snooped on her, I wouldn't have found out that she lied about her degree.

senses.definition: The act of snooping.
senses.example: After a quick snoop through my drawers, my sister admitted she had read my diary.

senses.definition: One who snoops.
senses.example: Be careful what you say around Gene because he's the bosses' snoop.

senses.definition: A private detective.
senses.example: She hired a snoop to find out if her husband was having an affair.

core.definition: To secretly look into or investigate someone's private affairs or belongings, usually without permission.

pronunciation.tip: Say one syllable with a long oo, the same vowel as in 'soup'. Release the final p clearly and don't shorten it to 'snop'.

nuance.connotation: Mostly negative, meaning intrusive; among friends it can be playful, as in 'Stop snooping!'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use snoop for poking into other people's private things, such as a drawer, a phone, or a coworker's computer. Playful lines like 'Are you snooping?' are common among friends and families. Snoop around is the usual phrase for looking through a place you shouldn't.

distinctions.note: Pry means asking intrusive personal questions or forcing something open; snoop involves secretly looking or searching.
Spy usually means gathering secret information for an organization or government; snoop is informal and small-scale.

examples.everyday: Did you snoop through my bag while I was at the gym?
examples.professional: IT staff should not snoop on employee email without a clear and published policy.
examples.analytical: Surveillance critics argue that when institutions snoop into private life, the burden of justification should fall on them.

nuance.analogy: Like a cat quietly peeking under the door to see what is in the next room.
nuance.etymology: Possibly from Dutch snoepen, to eat secretly; the connection is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Using snoop as a countable noun without an article, as in 'I did a snoop'; say 'I snooped' or 'I had a snoop around'.
Dropping the preposition: say snoop through the drawer or snoop around, not 'snoop the drawer'.

snoop.etymology: From Dutch *snoepen* (“to pry, eat in secret, sneak”) or maybe Old Norse *snópa* (“to idle about dismally”), or (“to use a blood found”).

senses.definition: Any of various concave objects (or portions of larger objects) that envelop a counterpart object.
senses.example: The ball joint fits snugly into its socket, so the arm moves freely in every direction.

senses.definition: An opening into which a plug or other connecting part is designed to fit (e.g. a light bulb socket).
The socket head for a socket wrench.
senses.example: I need a half-inch socket for this wrench to loosen the lug nuts.

senses.definition: A hollow tool for grasping and lifting tools dropped in a well-boring.
senses.example: The driller used a socket to retrieve the wrench that had fallen down the well.

senses.definition: The hollow of a candlestick.
senses.example: Melted wax dripped down the side and hardened inside the candlestick's socket.

senses.definition: One endpoint of a two-way communication link, used for interprocess communication across a network.
senses.example: Our logging daemon writes each event to a Unix domain socket for the monitoring service.

senses.definition: One endpoint of a two-way named pipe on Unix and Unix-like systems, used for interprocess communication.
senses.example: Our logging daemon writes each event to a Unix domain socket for the monitoring service.

senses.definition: A steel apparatus attached to a saddle to protect the thighs and legs.
senses.example: The old cavalry saddle had a steel socket to shield the rider's thighs and legs.

senses.definition: The vagina.
senses.example: The patient reported pain in the socket, so the doctor ordered an examination.

senses.definition: A hollow into a bone which a part fits, such as an eye, or another bone, in the case of a joint.
senses.example: The femoral head rests in the hip socket, allowing a wide range of motion.

senses.definition: To place or fit in a socket.
senses.example: Carefully socket the new bulb into the lamp before tightening the cover.

core.definition: A hole or device in a wall, fixture or appliance into which a plug or light bulb is inserted to make an electrical connection.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SAH, and say the second vowel as a short, reduced 'ih'. Do not add an extra syllable, and remember the t is quiet-ish and not flapped in this position.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday word for household and technical objects.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use socket for electrical outlets in the sense of a fitting for a bulb, and also for the sockets on tools and machines. For a wall outlet, most Americans say 'outlet' or 'plug' rather than socket, so 'socket' sounds more technical in that context. Context usually makes the meaning clear.

distinctions.note: An outlet is the wall receptacle where you plug things in; a socket is the fitting that holds a light bulb or the receiving part of a device.
A plug is the end of a cord that goes into a socket or outlet; plug and socket are complementary parts.

examples.everyday: The bulb won't work, so check whether it's screwed in tight to the socket.
examples.professional: We need a 12-volt socket on the control panel so the sensor can be powered during testing.
examples.analytical: Socket and plug connectors allow modular design, since each component can be replaced without rewiring the whole system.

nuance.analogy: A socket is like a catcher's mitt: it is shaped to receive exactly one kind of object and hold it securely.
nuance.etymology: From Old French soket, diminutive of soc, a plowshare, referring to a receiving part.
common_mistakes: Using socket for a wall outlet in ordinary American speech, where outlet is more common.
Adding an extra syllable, saying 'SOK-et' with a full vowel.
nuance.biblical_note: In Exodus the Hebrew word 'eden, meaning base or socket, names the foundation pieces of silver that held up the boards and pillars of the tabernacle. Exodus 26:19 describes the forty silver sockets under the twenty boards of the sanctuary, showing that the structure rested on firm, precious bases. Exodus 38:27 records that a hundred talents of silver went to casting the sockets of the sanctuary and of the veil, showing how carefully these bases were made.

socket.etymology: From Middle English *socket*, *soket*, from Anglo-Norman *soket* (“spearhead”), diminutive of Old French *soc* (“plowshare”), from Vulgar Latin **soccus*, a word borrowed, from **sukkos*, literally "pig's snout", from Proto-Indo-European **suH-*.

senses.definition: A sentimental fondness or affection.
senses.example: She had a soft spot for other people's hard-luck stories.

senses.definition: A point of vulnerability in a defense.
senses.example: The attackers quickly found a soft spot in the team's defense and scored twice.

senses.definition: A fontanelle.
senses.example: The pediatrician gently checked the baby's soft spot on top of her head.

core.definition: A special fondness or tender feeling you have for a person, animal, place or thing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SOFT in this compound, with spot lighter. Keep the t in soft clear, and do not add an extra vowel after it, since the final t of soft is a crisp stop.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it signals warmth and affection, often toward someone who seems tough or hard to like.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase casually about people, animals, places or ideas, as in I have a soft spot for old movies. It is almost always followed by for or in my heart, and it sounds friendly rather than formal. In sports or military talk it can mean a weak point, and in medicine it names the fontanelle on a baby's skull, but those meanings are less common in everyday talk. A natural reply is Me too or Oh, I know what you mean.

distinctions.note: A weak spot is a point of vulnerability or a weakness in someone's abilities or defenses, with no sense of affection.
A blind spot is an area where you fail to notice problems or your own errors, so it describes a gap in awareness rather than fondness.

collocations: a soft spot in my heart
a soft spot for old songs

examples.everyday: I know he can be grumpy, but I have a soft spot for him because he always helps my kids with their homework.
examples.professional: I have a soft spot for mentoring programs, so I'm glad to support the new pilot in the budget discussion.
examples.analytical: Sentimental attachment can create a soft spot for a favorite theory, which makes us less willing to weigh evidence against it.

nuance.analogy: A soft spot is like a worn patch on a leather chair: years of affection have made that one place tender, even when the rest of you is firm.
nuance.etymology: Soft comes from Old English softe; spot comes from Middle English spotte, meaning a small area or mark.
common_mistakes: Using to instead of for, as in a soft spot to my heart; say a soft spot for someone or a soft spot in my heart.
Using soft spot for any gentle surface; in everyday talk it is mainly used for emotional fondness.

senses.definition: In a solitary manner; alone.

core.definition: In a solitary way; alone, without company or in isolation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SAH. The 'r' is pronounced clearly, and the final '-ly' is spoken as 'lee,' not 'lie.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly wistful. It describes being alone, which can be peaceful or lonely depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'solitarily' in conversation; they say 'alone' or 'by myself.' It appears in literary descriptions, travel writing or formal descriptions of someone living or working by themselves. In casual speech, 'alone' is the natural choice.

distinctions.note: 'Alone' is everyday and flexible, while 'solitarily' is literary and emphasizes the manner of being alone.
'Lonely' describes an emotional state of sadness, while 'solitarily' describes a physical or social condition.

examples.everyday: Grandpa lives solitarily on the farm now, but he says he likes the quiet.
examples.professional: Most of the analysts work solitarily on their models, then meet to compare results.
examples.analytical: The poet describes the wanderer who walks solitarily through the valley, and the solitude becomes a form of thought.

nuance.analogy: Like a single lighthouse on a dark coast: it stands alone, but it is there to guide the ships that pass.
nuance.etymology: From 'solitary' (Latin 'solitarius', alone) plus the adverbial suffix '-ly'.
common_mistakes: Using 'solitarily' in casual speech where 'alone' or 'by myself' is more natural.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'suh-LIT-uh-rily,' which is a different pronunciation pattern.

senses.definition: One who lives alone, or in solitude; an anchorite, hermit or recluse.
Ellipsis of solitary confinement.
senses.example: The prisoners who started the riot were moved to solitary.

senses.definition: The state of being solitary; solitude.
Living or being by oneself; alone; having no companion present.
Performed, passed, or endured alone.
senses.example: a solitary journey

senses.definition: Not much visited or frequented; remote from society.
senses.example: a solitary residence or place

senses.definition: Not inhabited or occupied; without signs of inhabitants or occupation; desolate; deserted.
senses.example: the solitary desert

senses.definition: Gloomy; dismal, because of not being inhabited.
Single; individual; sole.
senses.example: a solitary example

senses.definition: Not associated with others of the same kind.

core.definition: Living or happening alone, without companions or other people around.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the first syllable, SAHL, with a weaker secondary stress on the 'tair' syllable. The final syllable is a light 'ee'; avoid pronouncing the middle vowel as a long 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound calm or peaceful in a positive context, or lonely and sad when describing someone isolated against their will.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use solitary in both everyday and literary speech, though 'alone' is more common in casual talk. The word often appears in phrases like 'solitary confinement' or 'a solitary walk'. Saying someone is 'solitary' can suggest they prefer being alone, which is a more neutral description than 'lonely'.

distinctions.note: Alone is the everyday word and can describe a temporary state; solitary is more formal and often suggests a chosen or lasting state of being apart from others.
Lonely describes an unhappy feeling of missing company, while solitary describes a situation or state without company and says nothing about feelings.

examples.everyday: I took a solitary walk along the lake this morning, and it was really relaxing.
examples.professional: Because the server is in a remote lab, the engineer works in solitary mode while the rest of the team is in another time zone.
examples.analytical: Thoreau's solitary life at Walden tests whether individual independence can coexist with the demands of community.

nuance.analogy: A solitary tree standing alone in an open field has no neighbors, but it is not necessarily sad; it is simply by itself.
nuance.etymology: From Latin solitarius, from solus 'alone'.
common_mistakes: Using solitary as a noun for a person without learning the older sense; in modern English 'loner' or 'hermit' is more natural.
Confusing solitary with solitude: solitary is the adjective, solitude is the noun.
Mispronouncing the middle syllables as 'sol-ih-TAIR-ee' instead of SAHL-ih-tair-ee.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Hebrew Bible, the idea of being solitary is expressed by yachid (יָחִיד), meaning 'only' or 'alone', often describing a single person or an only child. Psalm 68:6 says God gives the lonely a home and family. Psalm 25:16 is a prayer from one who is lonely and afflicted and asks God for mercy. Genesis 2:18 says it is not good for the man to be alone, so God makes a helper for him.

solitary.etymology: From Middle English *solitarie*, borrowed from Latin *sōlitārius*.

senses.definition: One who or that which solves.
senses.example: The first successful solver of the puzzle will win a prize.

core.definition: A person or program that solves problems, puzzles or equations.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SAHL, and make the final syllable a reduced, r-colored vowel, like the er in butter. Avoid pronouncing it sol-vur with a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It describes a tool or person that gets answers, without emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Solver is common in technical settings, such as an equation solver or a SAT solver in software. In everyday talk Americans more often say puzzle solver or problem solver. It is a neutral term that can describe a human or a program.

distinctions.note: A problem-solver is a person skilled at tackling problems in general, while a solver is more often a specific tool or a person who solves a particular kind of puzzle.
A solution is the answer itself, while a solver is the agent or program that produces it.

examples.everyday: My nephew is a great crossword solver; he finishes the Sunday puzzle in under an hour.
examples.professional: The optimization solver failed to converge, so we need to relax some of the constraints in the model.
examples.analytical: A SAT solver can decide whether a formula is satisfiable, but it does not by itself explain the structure behind the answer.

nuance.analogy: A solver is like a skilled locksmith: it takes a problem and works through the mechanism until the lock opens.
nuance.etymology: From solve plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using solver to mean the answer itself; the answer is the solution.
Saying sol-ver with a full vowel in the last syllable instead of a reduced r-colored sound.

senses.definition: Having no physical or organic cause.

core.definition: Describing physical symptoms that have no clear medical cause and are thought to arise from psychological factors.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SOH, and reduce the middle syllables to quick schwas. The final -form is pronounced clearly with an American r, not as form with a dropped r.

nuance.connotation: Clinical and potentially stigmatizing, since it implies that symptoms are not fully physical. Use it carefully with patients.
nuance.usage_note: Somatoform appears mainly in psychiatric and medical writing, including older DSM-IV terms such as somatoform disorder. Americans talking casually would say the symptoms might be stress-related. Because the term can imply the symptoms are not real, clinicians avoid it in conversation with patients.

distinctions.note: Psychosomatic describes a general link between mind and body, while somatoform is a diagnostic category for symptoms without a clear physical cause.
Somatic simply means relating to the body, while somatoform specifically means having the form of a physical illness without one.

examples.everyday: The doctor said my back pain might be somatoform, but I still wanted an MRI to be sure.
examples.professional: The team ruled out structural causes first, and the somatoform label was used only after a full neurological workup.
examples.analytical: A somatoform diagnosis raises a question about whether the absence of a physical cause is by itself enough basis for a psychological explanation.

nuance.analogy: Like a costume that looks exactly like a physical illness but is actually worn for psychological reasons.
nuance.etymology: From Greek soma, body, plus -form, from Latin forma, shape.
common_mistakes: Confusing somatoform with somatic; somatic is a general word for bodily, while somatoform is a specific diagnostic term.
Using somatoform to mean faked or imagined symptoms, which is inaccurate and can be hurtful.

senses.definition: An uncertain or unspecified thing; one thing.
senses.example: I must have forgotten to pack something, but I can't think what.

senses.definition: A quality to a moderate degree.
senses.example: The performance was something of a disappointment.

senses.definition: A talent or quality that is difficult to specify.
senses.example: She has a certain something.

senses.definition: Somebody who or something that is superlative or notable in some way.
senses.example: He's really something! I've never heard such a great voice.

senses.definition: Having a characteristic that the speaker cannot specify.
senses.example: The old painting had a something quality about it that I still cannot put into words.

senses.definition: Somewhat; to a degree.
senses.example: The baby looks something like his father.

senses.definition: Used to adverbialise a following adjective.
senses.example: I miss them something terrible/rotten. (I miss them terribly)

senses.definition: Designates an action whose name is forgotten by, unknown or unimportant to the user, e.g. from words of a song.
senses.example: We spent the whole afternoon somethinging the gutters, whatever that job is actually called.

senses.definition: An object whose nature is yet to be defined.
senses.example: Our sensors picked up something beneath the ice that nobody can yet explain or identify.

senses.definition: An object whose name is forgotten by, unknown or unimportant to the user, e.g. from words of a song. Also used to refer to an object earlier indefinitely referred to as 'something' (pronoun sense).
senses.example: Hand me that something on the counter, the little thingy you use for opening jars.

core.definition: An unspecified or unnamed thing; a thing that you do not need to name exactly or cannot name.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SUM, and make 'thing' with a short 'i' and a clear 'th'. The 'p' in parentheses is often dropped in speech, so say 'SUM-thing', not 'SUMP-thing'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound casual or vague, and it can be positive when used for a good quality ('She has something special').
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'something' constantly in everyday talk to point to an unnamed thing ('Something smells great'), and in conversation, 'something like that' means 'approximately' or 'or similar'. It is also used in phrases like 'or something' to sound casual or vague. In formal writing, use a more specific noun.

distinctions.note: 'Something' is used in positive statements, while 'anything' is used in negatives and questions ('Did you see anything?').
'Something like' means approximately or similar to, as in 'It's something like a cake'.

examples.everyday: Something smells great in the kitchen, so I think dinner is almost ready.
examples.professional: Something in the logs doesn't match what the dashboard is showing, so let's check the ingestion job.
examples.analytical: Something in the human person resists being reduced entirely to biology, and theology names that something the soul.

nuance.analogy: 'Something' is like a box with a label you have not read yet: you know there is an object inside, but not yet what it is.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'sum', meaning 'a certain', combined with 'thing'.
common_mistakes: Using 'something' in negative sentences where 'anything' is needed ('I don't see something' should be 'I don't see anything').
Adding a strong 'p' sound in the middle, saying 'SUMP-thing', which is not typical in careful General American speech.

something.etymology: From Middle English *somþyng*, *some-thing*, *som thing*, *sum thinge*, *sum þinge*, from Old English *sum* *þing*, equivalent to *some* + *thing*.

senses.definition: Synonym of sophistical, of or related to the ancient Sophists, characterized by fallacious reasoning.
senses.example: The philosopher dismissed the argument as sophistic, since its conclusion relied on clever word games.

senses.definition: (historical) The supposed beliefs and methods of the Sophists, taken as a kind of school of thought.
senses.example: Plato spent much of his career attacking what he saw as the sophistic tradition of teaching rhetoric for pay.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: Using clever but misleading arguments to win a debate, or relating to the ancient Greek Sophists.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, and keep the first syllable very weak. The ending is -ik, not -ick with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests arguments that look clever but are misleading or dishonest.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sophistic mainly in philosophy, classics, rhetoric and academic writing. In everyday speech they might say slippery, tricky or misleading. The word is formal and can sound stiff in casual conversation, so use it when discussing argument.

distinctions.note: Sophisticated means refined, worldly or complex, while sophistic means reasoning that deliberately misleads.
Sophistical is the more common synonym in modern academic writing, while sophistic is more formal and often used for the ancient Sophists.
Specious describes an argument that seems plausible but is false, while sophistic emphasizes deliberately clever but deceptive reasoning.

examples.everyday: Don't give me that sophistic excuse; just tell me what actually happened.
examples.professional: The proposal uses sophistic framing to hide the real cost, so we should ask for the numbers.
examples.analytical: Plato criticized the Sophists for using sophistic rhetoric that valued winning an argument over finding the truth.

nuance.analogy: Sophistic reasoning is like a card trick that looks fair but depends on a hidden move you were meant to miss.
nuance.etymology: From Greek sophistēs, meaning a wise person or expert, from sophos, wise.
common_mistakes: Confusing sophistic with sophisticated, which means refined or complex.
Using sophistic for any clever argument, when it specifically implies deception or misleading reasoning.

senses.definition: Saying you didn't hear or understand.

core.definition: A polite way to say you did not hear or understand what someone just said, so you need them to repeat it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SAHR and DID and KACH. Reduce didn't to a quick 'DID-unt' and let the t in catch be a clear t, not a flap. The words link together, so say it almost as one phrase.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to polite. It shows you are trying to understand, and it is less blunt than 'What?'
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this constantly on the phone, in meetings and in person when a voice is faint or a noisy room swallows a word. A natural reply is to repeat the sentence or say 'Oh, I said that the report is ready.' Saying just 'What?' sounds abrupt in most business and service settings.

distinctions.note: Pardon? is short and slightly more formal or British-sounding; Americans more often say 'Sorry?' or 'Excuse me?' in casual speech.
What? is blunt and can sound rude or impatient, while the full phrase signals politeness and apology.

collocations: Sorry, I didn't catch your name
I didn't catch the last part
Sorry, I didn't quite catch that

examples.everyday: Sorry, I didn't catch that. Did you say the store closes at nine?
examples.professional: Sorry, I didn't catch that last point about the deadline. Could you repeat it for the team?
examples.analytical: Sorry, I didn't catch that premise; could you restate the argument so I can evaluate the inference?

nuance.analogy: Like a ball thrown fast that you missed in the air; you politely ask for it to be thrown again.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I didn't got' instead of 'I didn't get'; here the idiom uses catch, not get, for hearing.
Pronouncing didn't with a long vowel, as in 'dih-dent' with a stressed second syllable.

conversation.text: Sorry, I didn't catch that. What was your last name?
"The code is 4471." "Sorry, I didn't catch that."

senses.definition: To organize or separate into groups, as a collection of items, so as to make tidy.
senses.example: Could you sort out your wardrobe and put the clothes you no longer use in one pile to give away and another to throw away?

senses.definition: To fix (a problem).
senses.example: The computer won't let me delete that file; could you sort it out?

senses.definition: To clarify by reviewing mentally.
senses.example: It's a bit confused at the moment, I'll try to sort it out later.

senses.definition: To arrange.
senses.example: Could you call Dave and sort out a meeting for tomorrow?

senses.definition: To separate from the remainder of a group; often construed with from.
senses.example: We need to sort out the problems we can solve from the ones we can't.

core.definition: To organize a messy group of things, or to solve or fix a problem so that it is no longer a problem.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on OUT, not on sort, in phrasal verbs like this. Keep the r in sort clear and let the t blend into the vowel of out, so it sounds like 'sor-TOWT'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It implies practical problem solving and tidy results.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sort out in both physical and abstract senses, such as 'Let me sort out the papers' or 'We need to sort out the billing error'. It is informal enough for everyday talk and common in business, though a formal report might prefer 'resolve' or 'organize'. Place a pronoun between sort and out, as in 'sort it out'.

distinctions.note: Figure out means to understand or discover something, while sort out means to organize or fix something.
Resolve is more formal and suits written reports, while sort out is conversational.

examples.everyday: Let me sort out the leftovers in the fridge before we eat.
examples.professional: I'll sort out the billing discrepancy with finance and send you the corrected invoice by Friday.
examples.analytical: The author never sorts out whether the category is descriptive or normative, which leaves the argument unresolved.

nuance.analogy: Like sorting a drawer of tangled cables until each one is in its own place.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on sort instead of out.
Placing a pronoun after out, as in 'sort out it'; the correct order is 'sort it out'.

conversation.text: I need to sort out my closet this weekend.
Don't worry, I'll sort it out with the bank.
Have you sorted out your visa problem yet?

senses.definition: That has deteriorated to the point of being unusable, unsafe, or inedible.
senses.example: We threw out the milk because it had spoiled in the warm kitchen overnight.

senses.definition: Heavily pampered; overindulged.
senses.example: The child was spoiled by constant gifts.

senses.definition: Selfish, greedy, or lazy due to pampering.
senses.example: My brother is spoiled and expects everyone to wait on him hand and foot.

core.definition: Food that has gone bad and is no longer safe or pleasant to eat, such as spoiled milk.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the single syllable, and the vowel is the diphthong in 'boy'. The final 'd' is clearly pronounced, so don't drop it before a word that begins with a consonant.

nuance.connotation: Negative when describing food or milk that has gone bad. When describing a person, it is mildly negative, suggesting excessive indulgence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'spoiled' for both food and children, and it is the standard spelling in American English. The British spelling 'spoilt' is mainly used in the UK, so an American would notice it as foreign. For food, people often say 'It's gone bad' in casual speech, while 'spoiled' sounds more standard. When talking about a child, calling them 'spoiled' is a common and fairly blunt criticism.

distinctions.note: 'Expired' refers to a date printed on packaging that has passed, while 'spoiled' means the food has actually deteriorated, which you can often tell by smell or taste.
'Rotten' is stronger and more vivid, describing food that has decayed badly, often with visible mold or a strong smell.

examples.everyday: Don't drink that milk, I think it's spoiled.
examples.professional: The cold storage unit failed overnight, so we had to throw out the spoiled inventory.
examples.analytical: Once the data pipeline is corrupted, every downstream report built on it is spoiled.

nuance.analogy: Like a fruit left out too long, something spoiled looks fine from afar but has quietly lost its quality.
nuance.etymology: From Old French 'espoillier', from Latin 'spoliare', to plunder or strip.
common_mistakes: Using 'spoilt' in American writing, which sounds British.
Confusing 'spoiled' (food or child) with 'spoiler' (a plot reveal or one who ruins something).

conversation.text: The milk is spoiled; it smells sour.
Don't eat that chicken; I think it's spoiled.
Their dog is so spoiled; it eats steak.

senses.definition: A ghost or phantom.
senses.example: The building was haunted by a couple of spooks.

senses.definition: A scare or fright.
senses.example: The big spider gave me a spook.

senses.definition: An undercover agent, spy, or intelligence analyst.
senses.example: The novel's protagonist is a retired spook who is pulled back for one last mission.

senses.definition: A metaphysical manifestation; an artificial distinction or construct.
senses.example: Critics argue that the concept of a fixed national identity is a spook created by nineteenth-century politics.

senses.definition: A player who engages in hole carding by attempting to glimpse the dealer's hole card when the dealer checks under an ace or a 10 to see if a blackjack is present.
senses.example: The surveillance camera caught the spook craning his neck to read the dealer's hole card.

senses.definition: A psychiatrist.
senses.example: He hated seeing the spook every Tuesday, though the medication had clearly helped his sleep.

senses.definition: (dated) A black person.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To frighten or make nervous (especially by startling).
senses.example: The hunters were spooked when the black cat crossed their path. The movement in the bushes spooked the deer and they ran.

senses.definition: To become frightened (by something startling).
senses.example: The deer spooked at the sound of the dogs.

senses.definition: To haunt.
senses.example: The memory of that cold winter still spooks me every time I hear the creaking attic door.

core.definition: A ghost or phantom, often used playfully in conversation about Halloween or spooky houses.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the long 'oo' of 'book' and 'look', and the final 'k' is a clear, unvoiced stop with no added vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral or playful as a ghost. Spook as a slur for Black people is deeply offensive, so avoid that usage entirely.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use spook in casual talk about ghosts, Halloween and haunted houses, and as a verb meaning to startle, as in 'the thunder spooked the dog'. The word is also informal slang for a spy, from Cold War films, but a common and offensive racial slur also uses this word, so avoid that sense in conversation.

distinctions.note: Ghost is the standard, neutral word; spook is more informal and playful, often used for a silly or startling apparition.
Scare is the general word for making someone afraid; spook suggests a sudden startle, often with a sense of unease.

collocations: the house is full of spooks

examples.everyday: The loud thunder spooked the dog, so he hid under the bed.
examples.professional: Don't spook the client with a surprise price increase; give them a heads-up first.
examples.analytical: The novel uses faint spooks at the edge of the story to make the reader doubt what is real.

nuance.analogy: Like a sudden creak in an empty house, a spook is a jolt that makes you look twice.
nuance.etymology: From Dutch spook, ghost, related to Low German spōk.
common_mistakes: Using spook in the racial slur sense or the spy sense without knowing its offensive history.
Confusing spook (a ghost or to startle) with spooky (an adjective meaning eerie).

spook.etymology: Borrowed from Dutch *spook* (“ghost”), from Middle Dutch *spooc* (“spook, ghost”), from **spōk*, ultimately from **spōk*.

senses.definition: At an occasional, infrequent, or irregular frequency.

core.definition: Occasionally and irregularly, at uneven intervals with no fixed pattern.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on -AD, the second syllable. The first syllable is a weak, rhotic 'er' sound, and the final -ly is a light 'lee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sporadically in reports, reviews, and written descriptions of irregular activity, such as a service that works sporadically. In speech people often choose 'on and off' or 'every now and then' instead. It sounds slightly formal, so use it in writing or professional contexts.

distinctions.note: Occasionally is everyday and suggests a few times here and there; sporadically sounds more formal and stresses irregular timing.
Periodically means at regular, predictable intervals, the opposite of sporadically.

examples.everyday: The Wi-Fi in the apartment still drops sporadically, so I usually reboot the router.
examples.professional: The API has been failing sporadically since Tuesday, so I'm adding logging to catch the next occurrence.
examples.analytical: The phenomenon appears sporadically across the sample, which complicates any claim about a stable underlying mechanism.

nuance.analogy: Like a porch light with a loose wire, it flickers on and off with no schedule.
nuance.etymology: From sporadic plus the adverb suffix -ally, from Greek sporadikos, 'scattered.'
common_mistakes: Placing the stress on the first syllable, 'SPOR-ad-ically.'
Using it to mean 'frequently,' which is the opposite of its meaning.

senses.definition: Typical of spring (the season).
senses.example: It was a warm, clear, springlike day, though it was still the middle of December.

senses.definition: Resembling a spring (coiled-shaped usually metal object).
senses.example: The old toy had a springlike coil of wire that bounced when pressed.

core.definition: Having the mild, fresh and pleasant qualities of spring, such as warmer air and new growth.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on SPRING, with a lighter secondary stress on -like. Don't stress -like as strongly as the first syllable, and keep the 'ing' short.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests warmth, freshness and renewal, usually about weather, places or moods.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use springlike mainly for weather, such as 'springlike temperatures' in a forecast, and for a warm day or a garden. In American spelling it is usually written as one closed word, 'springlike', rather than with a hyphen. It does not mean bouncy; for that, use springy.

distinctions.note: Springy means bouncy or quick to return to shape; springlike means having the qualities of the spring season.
Vernal is formal or literary and mainly used in poetry or technical writing; springlike is the everyday American word.

examples.everyday: It feels springlike outside, so let's open the windows for a while.
examples.professional: The forecast shows springlike temperatures across the region, so we can move the outdoor sales meeting to Thursday.
examples.analytical: The poet's springlike images of renewal set the stage for the poem's turn toward grief.

nuance.analogy: Like a warm breeze after a long winter, springlike describes the first thaw of the year.
nuance.etymology: From spring (the season) plus -like.
common_mistakes: Confusing springlike with springy, which means bouncy, and using it to describe a coiled spring object.
Writing it with a hyphen as 'spring-like', which is less common in American usage.

senses.definition: A person who is fair, trustworthy, or forthright; a person who bargains or transacts business in a fair, honest manner.
senses.example: My grandfather was a square shooter who never cheated his customers at the feed store.

core.definition: An honest, fair, and straightforward person whose dealings can be trusted.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on shoot, so say SHOO-ter with a long oo sound. The final -er is weak and sounds like schwa-r, and square is lightly stressed.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises someone's honesty and fairness, especially in business, sports, and trade.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use square shooter for someone who keeps their word and deals fairly, such as a car dealer, a coach, or a business partner. The phrase is somewhat old-fashioned and folksy, so it can sound affectionate or a little dated. A natural reply is 'That's good to hear, because you don't meet many of those.'

distinctions.note: Straight shooter means essentially the same thing, honest and direct, and is more common in modern American speech than square shooter.
Square deal is a noun for fair treatment in a transaction, while square shooter describes the honest person who gives it.
Honest broker is a more formal term for a neutral mediator who helps others reach agreement, while square shooter is a casual compliment for personal integrity.

examples.everyday: My mechanic is a square shooter; he tells you what's really wrong and doesn't pad the bill.
examples.professional: Our sales director is a square shooter, so clients trust her quotes without asking for a second opinion.
examples.analytical: Trust in markets depends on the presence of square shooters who keep their word even when keeping it costs them money.

nuance.analogy: A square shooter is like a referee who calls the game straight, favoring neither team.
common_mistakes: Using square shooter to describe an athlete's shooting accuracy; the phrase describes character, not skill.
Using very in front, as in 'very square shooter', which sounds unnatural; say 'a real square shooter' or 'a straight shooter'.

senses.definition: The property of being stagnant.
senses.example: The stagnancy of wages over the past decade has frustrated many young workers.

core.definition: The state of being stuck and not moving, growing, or developing, especially in an economy, a career, or a relationship.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, STAG, and the middle syllable is a weak schwa, so say STAG-nun-see, not stag-NAN-see. The final -cy sounds like see.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it implies a lack of progress, energy, or change, and it is often used for economies, careers, or ideas.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stagnancy when describing a long period of little progress, such as wages, the economy, or a career, often in news, business writing, or essays. Stagnation is more common in everyday speech, while stagnancy stresses the state itself. In casual talk, people often say things feel stuck or stagnant.

distinctions.note: Stagnation is the more common word for a period of little growth, especially economic; stagnancy stresses the state of being stagnant.
A stalemate is a deadlock between opposing sides; stagnancy describes a general lack of movement without necessarily involving an opponent.

examples.everyday: I'm tired of the stagnancy in my job; I've been doing the same thing for years.
examples.professional: The quarterly report shows wage stagnancy in our target markets despite strong productivity gains.
examples.analytical: Many critics argue that institutional stagnancy, rather than individual laziness, explains why reform efforts keep failing.

nuance.analogy: Like water in a pond with no current, it grows still, murky, and eventually starts to smell.
nuance.etymology: From Latin stagnare (to be stagnant), from stagnum (standing water or pool).
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in stag-NAN-see; the stress belongs on the first syllable.
Using stagnancy for a temporary pause; it describes a lasting state of little movement or growth.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to starch.
Containing starch.
Having the quality of fabric starch as applied to fabric; stiff, hard; starched.
senses.example: The collar of his new shirt felt starchy and stiff against his neck.

senses.definition: Having a starched personality; stiffly formal.

core.definition: Containing a lot of starch, such as potatoes, rice, bread or pasta; or describing a stiff, formal manner.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final '-y' is a clear 'ee' sound. Do not pronounce it as 'STAR-chuh' or 'STAR-chih'.

nuance.connotation: Often neutral in food talk, but sometimes negative in diet discussions; the stiff-manner sense is formal and somewhat negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'starchy' mainly about foods, especially in conversations about diets and carbohydrates, where it can sound slightly negative. The sense of stiff, prim or formal behavior is less common and sounds old-fashioned. For the clothing sense, people usually say 'starched'.

distinctions.note: Starchy describes food or formal manners; starched describes fabric that has been treated with starch.
Stiff is a general term for rigidity; starchy adds a sense of formality or prim manner.

examples.everyday: I try to limit starchy foods like bread and rice at dinner, but I still love potatoes.
examples.professional: The nutrition team flagged the starchy sides on the cafeteria menu and suggested more vegetables.
examples.analytical: The region's starchy staple crops shaped its agricultural calendar and its distribution of labor across the seasons.

nuance.analogy: Starchy foods are like a storage room packed with dense, floury energy, ready to be used when needed.
nuance.etymology: From 'starch' with the suffix '-y', meaning full of or resembling starch.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -y as 'uh' or 'ih' rather than the clear 'ee' sound.
Using 'starchy' for clothes, where 'starched' is the correct word.

senses.definition: A political entity that regulates society and the population within a definite territory.
senses.example: Each state in the federation sets its own rules for voter registration.

senses.definition: The current governing political entity in which the speaker lives.
senses.example: I pay state income tax, and I have lived in this state for ten years.

core.definition: A nation or major political division with its own government and laws, such as one of the fifty U.S. states.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first and only syllable, with a clear diphthong 'ay' like in 'day'. The final t is light, and in fast speech it can sound close to a flap or drop before a consonant.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word describes a political fact, and it becomes emotional only in context, such as patriotism or government power.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually mean one of the fifty U.S. states when they say 'state' in everyday talk, as in 'I'm moving to another state.' They capitalize 'State' when it names a specific entity, such as the State Department or the State of Texas, but use lowercase for general references like 'state law.' In political or academic writing, 'the State' can mean the government as an institution.

distinctions.note: A country is the nation as a whole, while a state is a political unit, either a national government or one of the divisions of a federal country.
A nation is a people who share an identity, while a state is a political institution with authority and borders.
Government is the body that runs the state, while state is the broader entity that includes its territory, people, and laws.

examples.everyday: I'm moving to another state next summer, so I'm packing everything.
examples.professional: Our company needs a license in every state where we deliver products.
examples.analytical: Hobbes argued that the state arises when individuals surrender certain rights to a sovereign authority.

nuance.analogy: A state is like a shared house with its own rules, which everyone living inside must follow.
nuance.etymology: From Latin status, meaning condition or standing, through Old French estat.
common_mistakes: Capitalizing 'state' in general use, as in 'a State law' instead of 'a state law'.
Using 'state' and 'country' interchangeably when talking about a U.S. state, which is a division of the country rather than a country itself.

senses.definition: The state or condition of being stateful.

core.definition: In software engineering, the quality of a system that remembers information from past interactions and uses it in later ones.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The '-ful' ending is reduced to 'fuhl', not pronounced as the full word 'full', and the last syllable is a weak 'nuhs'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a technical description of system design, with no positive or negative judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'statefulness' almost only in software engineering, networking, and distributed systems discussions. In everyday English, people would describe a person's emotional state or condition instead. Engineers usually say 'stateful' as an adjective more often than the noun.

distinctions.note: Persistence means data survives restarts or shutdowns, while statefulness means the system keeps context between interactions, even if only in memory.
A session is one specific mechanism for keeping state for a user, while statefulness is the general property.

examples.everyday: My friend who codes says the app needs some statefulness so it remembers what is in my cart.
examples.professional: We need statefulness in the chat service so users can resume a conversation after a dropped connection.
examples.analytical: Debates about statefulness in distributed systems often come down to where context is stored and who is responsible for it.

nuance.analogy: A stateful waiter remembers your order, while a stateless one makes you repeat it at every table visit.
nuance.etymology: From 'state' plus the suffixes '-ful' (full of) and '-ness' (quality of).
common_mistakes: Using 'statefulness' to mean a person's mood or condition in everyday talk.
Stressing '-ful' as a full word 'full' instead of the reduced American ending.

senses.definition: A person who compiles, interprets, or studies statistics.
A mathematician with a specialty of statistics.
senses.example: The statistician built a model to predict which patients would relapse.

core.definition: A person whose job is to collect, analyze, and interpret numerical data using statistical methods.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the STISH syllable, and the ending -ian is weak. The ti is pronounced as sh, and learners often stress the first syllable or say the ending as ee-an.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests expertise, rigor, and objectivity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use statistician for people who work at agencies like the Census Bureau, in pharmaceutical trials, insurance, sports analytics, and academic research. In a company, people may say data scientist instead, which has a broader meaning that includes programming. Statistician is a respected professional title and is usually said with respect.

distinctions.note: A statistician focuses on the theory of inference and uncertainty, while a data scientist often combines statistics with programming and engineering.
An actuary assesses financial risk for insurance and pensions, usually with professional certification, while a statistician may work in any field.
A statist is a supporter of state control; the two words look similar but have completely different meanings.

collocations: a statistician at the Census Bureau

examples.everyday: My sister is a statistician, so she always checks whether a news headline is really supported by the numbers.
examples.professional: I asked the statistician on our team to review the A/B test before we ship the change.
examples.analytical: The statistician's role is to make explicit the assumptions behind any inference from a sample to a population.

nuance.analogy: A statistician is like a referee for numbers, deciding whether the evidence really supports the claim being made.
nuance.etymology: From statistics plus the suffix -ian, meaning one who practices or is skilled in a field.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in STAT-ih-stish-un, instead of the STISH syllable.
Confusing statistician with statist, which means a supporter of state control.

senses.definition: To remain where one is, whilst others leave.
senses.example: Half the team left for lunch, but Maria stayed behind to finish the report.

senses.definition: To remain in a classroom or school at the end of teaching, especially to receive punishment.
Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see stay,‎ behind.

core.definition: To remain in a place after others have left, or to remain in a classroom after school, often as a punishment.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on HIND, so the first syllable of 'behind' is weak and short, like 'bih'. Don't stress 'be', and keep the final d clear before a following word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when people remain to finish a task; negative when used for school punishment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say a person 'stayed behind' when they did not leave with the group, such as 'Two of us stayed behind to lock up.' In school, being made to stay behind usually means detention or being kept after class as a consequence. For after-hours work, 'stay late' is the more natural everyday phrase.

distinctions.note: Stay behind focuses on not leaving with others, while stay back often focuses on keeping a physical distance from something.
Stay behind is an active choice to remain, while be left behind is passive and suggests someone was not taken along.

collocations: stay behind for a few minutes

examples.everyday: Can you stay behind and watch the dog while we run to the store?
examples.professional: I'll stay behind after the stand-up to walk the product team through the outage report.
examples.analytical: Many historians argue that the people who stayed behind in occupied towns shaped postwar memory as much as those who fled.

nuance.analogy: Like the last guest who lingers at a party after everyone else has said goodnight.
common_mistakes: Saying 'stay behind from class' instead of 'stay behind after class'.
Confusing the active phrase with the passive 'be left behind'.

senses.definition: Pertaining to a stereotype; conventional.
senses.example: Critics said the film relied on stereotypical characters and predictable romantic plots.
